notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 Bb4, White should not play dxe5? because …Nxe4 wins a pawn. Instead, d5 is a solid alternative, closing the center and gaining space, though it allows Black to play for a win.
notes.teaches: When facing a pin on the knight, avoid premature captures that open the center. Pushing d5 can be a good way to seize space and limit the opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to e3 or g5, castle kingside, and aim for a kingside attack with moves like h3, g3, and later f4.

notes.explains: After d5 Ne7, White should not play Nxe5? because …Nxe4 Nxe4 Qe7 forks the knight and pawn. Instead, Bd3 develops and protects the d3-pawn, preparing to meet ...Bxc3+ with bxc3, accepting doubled pawns but gaining the bishop pair and a potential c4 push.
notes.teaches: Accepting doubled pawns can be worthwhile if you get the bishop pair and central control. The c4 pawn can later support the center and restrict Black's queenside play.
notes.plans: White will castle, play h3 to prevent ...Bg4, then continue with Be3, Qd2, and prepare a kingside expansion with g3 and f4.

notes.explains: With a closed center, the value of individual moves is reduced; the focus is on the overall plan. White plays h3 to prevent ...Bg4, then will develop the bishop to e3 and prepare a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, prioritize long-term plans over precise move orders. The key is to have the right setup and general idea.
notes.plans: White will play Be3, Qd2, Kh2 (prophylaxis against ...Nh5), then g3, Nf3-d2 or Ng1, and eventually f4 to break open the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays Kh2 to prepare g3, which would answer ...Nh5? (threatening ...Nf4) by allowing g3 without fear of ...Bxh3. The king move is both prophylactic and aggressive, as it also prepares to move the knight from f3 and push f4.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic king moves can serve dual purposes: preventing enemy threats and enabling your own plans. Here, Kh2 neutralizes ...Nh5 and sets up g3 and f4.
notes.plans: After Kh2, White will play g3, then move the knight from f3 (e.g., Nd2 or Ng1) and push f4 to open lines on the kingside.

notes.explains: After Black retreats the knight to f6, White plays Ng1 to protect h3 and prepare f4. This retreat is not passive; it ties Black's queen to d7 if she tries to attack h3, creating a mutual passivity.
notes.teaches: A knight on g1 defending h3 can be a useful defensive resource. If Black's queen goes to d7 to attack h3, both pieces become tied down, but White is happy with that trade-off.
notes.plans: White will now aim for f4, but must be careful of tactical counterplay. If f4 is not immediately feasible, White may switch to h4 to expand on the kingside.

notes.explains: When f4 is not tactically sound (due to ...exf4 gxf4 f5! attacking the e3-bishop), White switches to h4. This move prepares h5 to kick the knight from g6, and also allows the knight on g1 to move without worrying about the h3-pawn (since ...Qh3+ is no longer a capture).
notes.teaches: If one plan fails tactically, be ready to switch to another. H4 is a healthy positional move that improves the kingside and can later support a bishop on g5.
notes.plans: White will push h5, forcing ...Nh8, then consider f3 and g4 to further constrict Black, or prepare a knight maneuver to e6.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nf4, a strong move that attacks the bishop on d3. White must calculate carefully: if Bxf4 exf4, then Black has ...Qh4+ and ...Qg5+ with perpetual check. White's best is Bxc5 first, then …bxc6 Bxf4 exf4, and now the bishop is not hanging, allowing White to bring the queen to f3 for defense.
notes.teaches: When facing a tactical sequence, consider the order of captures. Taking on c5 first can remove a defender or change the dynamics, giving you an extra tempo to organize your defense.
notes.plans: After Bxc5 bxc6 Bxf4 exf4, White will play Qf3, defending f4 and preparing to consolidate. Black's attack may fizzle if White can trade pieces and activate the rooks.

notes.explains: White plays Qf3, defending the f4-pawn and preparing to meet ...Bg4 with Qxf4 (since the queen is protected by the knight on g1). Black's attack is neutralized, and White's king is safe.
notes.teaches: In defensive positions, centralizing the queen can protect multiple weak points and prepare counterattacks. The knight on g1 is a key defender of h3 and g5.
notes.plans: White will consolidate by trading pieces, activating the rooks (e.g., Re1, Re6), and eventually counterattacking on the queenside or converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black tries ...Bg4, but White's queen takes on f4 (protected by the knight). After ...Bh3, White's knight returns to g1, and Black's checks are blocked by ...Nh3. White's queen drops back to g2, and Black's attack runs out of steam.
notes.teaches: When defending against a queen check, look for knight blocks that also protect key squares. The knight on g1/h3 is a versatile defender.
notes.plans: White will continue to consolidate, perhaps with Re1, and then look to activate the rook on h1 or push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: After Black's attack fizzles, White plays Re1, a simple improving move that gets the rook onto an open file. There is no deep idea; just general activation.
notes.teaches: When the position is unclear, improving your worst-placed piece (here the rook) is a good principle. Don't always look for tactical fireworks.
notes.plans: White will continue to improve piece coordination, perhaps with Re6, and then look to trade queens or launch a counterattack.

notes.explains: White plays Re6, an indirect defense: it threatens Rg6+ and also prepares Qe4. If Black plays ...g5, White has Rg6+ picking up the pawn. This move uses tactics to defend while counterattacking.
notes.teaches: Indirect defense can be more effective than passive protection. By threatening counterplay, you force the opponent to respect your threats.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Qe4, threatening mate on g6, and then trade queens or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays Qe4, threatening Qxg6 and Rg8#. Black's king is exposed, and White's pieces coordinate for a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is weak, centralize your queen and use rook lifts to create mating threats. Tactical awareness is crucial to finish the game.
notes.plans: White will continue with checks and threats, eventually forcing queen trade or checkmate.

notes.explains: White forces queen trade with Qc8+ and then captures on g4, leaving White a piece up. The rest is technique.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify by trading queens and eliminate counterplay. Then convert with careful technique.
notes.plans: White will activate the king, bring the knight into play, and use rook and knight to deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: In the Four Knights Scotch (e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 Bb4), the best move is Nxe5! instead of d5. After …Nxe4 Qg4! (forking the knight and pawn), White gets a strong attack. This is similar to the Sicilian Pin Variation.
notes.teaches: When a knight is pinned, look for queen sorties like Qg4 to exploit the pin and create threats. The key is to attack the pinned piece and the pawn simultaneously.
notes.plans: After Qg4, White threatens Qxg7 and also attacks the knight on e4. Black must defend carefully, often leading to a pawn-up endgame for White.

notes.explains: In the line Nxe5 Nxe4 Qg4 Nxc3 a3 Ba5 bxc3 d5 Qxg7, Black may try …Rf8, but White plays Bh6! with a strong attack. If …g6, then Bxf8 Kxf8 and White is up an exchange.
notes.teaches: After winning a pawn, look to trade off the opponent's active pieces and exploit the dark-square weaknesses. Bh6 is a typical move to disrupt Black's coordination.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qg4 or Qf6, targeting f7 and g7, and eventually consolidate the material advantage.

notes.explains: If Black plays …Qe7 instead of …Nxc3, White can still play Qxg7, and after …Rf8, the discovered check is again harmless. White can play a3 Ba5 b4 Bb6 Bb2, and Black's position is difficult.
notes.teaches: The Qg4 motif works even if Black tries to defend with the queen. The key is to stay alert to tactical opportunities and not be afraid to capture on g7.
notes.plans: White will develop quickly, castle queenside, and launch a kingside attack with g4 and h4.

notes.explains: In the line Nxe5 Nxe4 Qg4 Nxc3 a3 Ba5 bxc3 Qe7 Qd4! (defending d5 and attacking the bishop), White is slightly better. After …d6 Qxe5 dxe5 Ba3, White has the bishop pair and better pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When the queen is forced to move, centralize it to control key squares and support your pawns. Qd4 here defends d5 and attacks the bishop, forcing Black to weaken the center.
notes.plans: White will play Ba3, castle queenside, and use the bishop pair to pressure Black's pawns.

notes.explains: If Black plays …d5 in the Nxe5 line, White can play Qg4! again, forking the knight on e4 and the pawn on g7. After …Nxc3 a3 Ba5 bxc3, White is up a pawn with a strong position.
notes.teaches: The Qg4 fork is a recurring theme in these lines. Always consider it when the knight on f6 is pinned and the e4-pawn is undefended.
notes.plans: White will consolidate with c3, develop the bishop, and enjoy a material advantage.

notes.explains: In the closed center position after d5, Black's plan is to play ...Nh5 and ...f5, similar to the King's Indian Defense. White must be careful not to allow ...f5 too early, as it can lead to a strong attack for Black.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, recognize typical pawn breaks. Black's ...f5 is a key counterplay, and White should prepare to meet it with moves like Ng5 or g4.
notes.plans: White should consider Ng5 to pressure the knight on h5 and prepare e6, or play g4 to prevent ...f5.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...f5 prematurely, White can respond with Ng5! attacking the knight on h5 and threatening e6. Black's best is to sacrifice the exchange on f3, but White gets a strong position.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside, look for knight jumps to e6 or g5 to exploit the weaknesses. Ng5 is a typical idea in King's Indian structures.
notes.plans: After Ng5, White will take on f5, then consider e6 or g4 to further constrict Black.

notes.explains: In the position after ...Nh5, White should consider Ng5 instead of g4. The move g4 weakens the f4 square and allows Black to play ...f5 with counterplay. Ng5 is more precise, threatening e6 and forcing Black to defend.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two plans, calculate the tactical consequences. g4 may seem natural but can be refuted; Ng5 is a more accurate way to punish Black's knight placement.
notes.plans: White will play Ng5, then e6 or f4, depending on Black's response.

notes.explains: In the game, White played h4 to switch plans. This is a good example of flexibility: when one plan (f4) fails, find another (h4-h5) to improve your position.
notes.teaches: Don't get fixated on one plan. If it doesn't work tactically, look for alternative ways to improve your position, even if they seem less obvious.
notes.plans: After h4, White will push h5, then consider f3 and g4, or prepare a knight maneuver to e6.

notes.explains: In the tactical phase after ...Nf4, White correctly played Bxc5 first to remove a defender and gain a tempo. This allowed White to bring the queen to f3 and defend.
notes.teaches: In complex tactical positions, the order of captures matters. Removing a defender first can give you an extra move to organize your defense.
notes.plans: After Bxc5 bxc5 Bxf4 exf4 Qf3, White is safe and can consolidate.

notes.explains: White's idea of Re6 was an indirect defense: it threatened Rg6+ and also prepared Qe4. This is a good example of using counterplay to defend.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for moves that create threats of your own. This forces the opponent to respect your counterplay and can relieve pressure.
notes.plans: After Re6, White will play Qe4, threatening mate and forcing Black to defend.

notes.explains: In the endgame, White used the king actively and coordinated rook and knight to deliver checkmate. The knight on g5 was particularly strong, hitting the rook and threatening mate.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate your king and use your pieces in coordination. A knight and rook can create mating threats even with few pawns.
notes.plans: White will continue to improve piece placement, target Black's king, and eventually force checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3 instead of the main line Bxc6. This is a third-rate move that allows Black to develop normally.
notes.teaches: Against the Rossolimo, choose a setup consistent with your usual Sicilian defense. Accelerated Dragon players should fianchetto the kingside.
notes.plans: Black will play Bg7 and develop naturally, aiming for a structure similar to the Accelerated Dragon.

notes.explains: Black has two main setups: Nf6 or the 'Batmanic' setup with e6/e5 and Ne7. Nf6 is simpler and solid.
notes.teaches: The Batmanic setup (Bg7, e6/e5, Ne7) avoids piece congestion but requires care against e5 pushes. Nf6 is more straightforward.
notes.plans: Black chooses Nf6, keeping options open.

notes.explains: White trades on c6, damaging Black's pawn structure but giving Black the bishop pair. Black should recapture with the d-pawn to open lines and control d4.
notes.teaches: When recapturing on c6, taking with the d-pawn is usually better: it opens the diagonal for the queen and improves central control.
notes.plans: Black plays dxc6, then develops with Bg7 and castles.

notes.explains: After dxc6, Black has a solid structure. The doubled pawns on c6 actually protect d5, a key central square.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns can be a positional asset if they control important squares and are not easily attacked.
notes.plans: Black will develop, castle, and later expand on the queenside with a6 and b5, or push e5 to gain space.

notes.explains: White plays passive moves like h3 and Bf1, doing nothing productive. Black can choose between d5 (ambitious) or d6 (solid, Sicilian-style).
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays passively, you can either punish them with an aggressive central break or maintain solid development and wait for them to overextend.
notes.plans: Black chooses d6, completing the Accelerated Dragon setup and preparing queenside expansion.

notes.explains: Black has completed development. The typical plan is queenside expansion with a6 and b5, followed by Bb7. This gains space and creates a good post for the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: In closed Sicilian structures, queenside expansion (a6, b5, Bb7) is a standard plan that increases space and improves piece activity.
notes.plans: Play a6, then b5, then Bb7. If White prevents b5 with a4, play Rb8 and prepare b5 with moves like Qa5.

notes.explains: White plays a4 to stop b5. Black should not abandon the plan; instead, play Rb8 and prepare b5 with moves like Qa5.
notes.teaches: If your opponent prevents your expansion with a4, don't give up the idea. Use prophylactic moves like Rb8 and Qa5 to support the b5 push.
notes.plans: Play Rb8, then Qa5, and eventually b5 when possible.

notes.explains: Black completes development with Be7. The bishop on e7 may look passive, but if the center opens, it can become powerful.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to play b4. Complete development first; the bishop on e7 is fine and may later become active after central breaks like d5.
notes.plans: Play Be7, then consider d5 or other central breaks.

notes.explains: White threatens Bh6, which would trade off Black's important dark-squared bishop. Black meets this with Rc8, preparing to respond to Bh6 with Bh8, keeping the bishop.
notes.teaches: In fianchetto positions, preserving the dark-squared bishop is often worth concessions. The typical antidote to Bh6 is to play Rc8 and meet Bh6 with Bh8.
notes.plans: If White plays Bh6, respond with Bh8. Do not allow the trade unless necessary.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, opening the center. If White takes on c5, Black recaptures on e4 and has active pieces. If White pushes e5, Black can play Nd7 or d4.
notes.teaches: When White has relaxed control over d5, a central break with d5 is often strong. Calculate the tactical consequences: if Bxc5, then dxe4; if e5, then Nd7 or d4.
notes.plans: After d5, if exd5, recapture with the knight and maintain pressure. If e5, consider Nd7 (attacking the pawn) or d4 (counter-attacking the bishop).

notes.explains: White pushes e5. Black plays Nd7, threatening the pawn. White can try e6, sacrificing a pawn to ruin Black's structure, but Black can avoid this with d4.
notes.teaches: When your knight attacks an advanced pawn, be aware of potential pawn sacrifices that damage your structure. Sometimes it's better to counter-attack with d4 instead of retreating.
notes.plans: After e5, Nd7 is natural. If e6, consider d4 to keep the bishop and avoid structural damage.

notes.explains: White plays e6 and Ng5, attacking the e6 pawn. Black must decide how to defend: push e5 (giving up the dark-squared bishop) or play d4 (creating a hole on e4 but keeping the bishop).
notes.teaches: In such positions, keeping the dark-squared bishop is often worth a structural concession. d4 creates a hole on e4 but preserves the bishop and maintains the pawn advantage.
notes.plans: Black plays d4, attacking the bishop, then retreats the knight to f8 to defend e6. This keeps the bishop and maintains the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays d4 and Nf8, defending e6. White's knight on g5 is annoying, so Black plays e5 to restrict it and prevent Nf4.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like e5 can restrict the opponent's knight and improve your position. Always consider your opponent's best square and try to take it away.
notes.plans: Play e5, then prepare to deal with White's knight on e4. The knight on f8 can reroute to d7 via b8 (Frankfurt airport maneuver).

notes.explains: White's knight heads to e4. Black plays Rc8, defending the c5 pawn prophylactically. The rook on c8 is safe and prepares to meet Ne4 with Nb8, rerouting to d7.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's knight threatens an outpost, use prophylactic moves like Rc8 to defend weaknesses. The 'Frankfurt airport' maneuver (Nb8-d7) is a classic way to redeploy a poorly placed knight.
notes.plans: If Ne4, play Nb8, then Nd7, reinforcing c5 and e5, and potentially contesting the e4 knight with Nf6.

notes.explains: White plays f4, opening the center. Black's pawns are undoubled, and the queen can come to d5. White threatens Qf7, but Black can defend with Qd5.
notes.teaches: When the center opens, be alert to tactical threats like Qf7. Defend with your queen or king, and consider counterplay.
notes.plans: Black plays exf4, then Qd5, defending f7 and centralizing the queen.

notes.explains: Black's queen on d5 protects f7 and is well placed. White may try Bh6 to trade bishops, but Black can respond with Bh8 or even sacrifice the exchange to keep the bishop.
notes.teaches: In dragon-like positions, preserving the dark-squared bishop is paramount. Sometimes sacrificing the exchange (Rxf8) is worth it to keep the bishop, especially if White has castled queenside.
notes.plans: If Bh6, play Bh8. If White takes on f8, Black has compensation with the bishop pair and attacking chances.

notes.explains: White plays Bh6, threatening to trade bishops. Black should respond with Bh8, keeping the bishop. However, Black blunders with Ne6, allowing a forced mate.
notes.teaches: Always check your opponent's replies. Tunnel vision on a tactical idea can cause you to miss simple threats like Qf7#.
notes.plans: The correct move is Bh8. After Ne6??, White has Qf7#.

notes.explains: Black blunders a forced mate. The move Ne6 cuts the queen's defense of f7, allowing Qf7#. This is a classic example of tunnel vision.
notes.teaches: After calculating a line, always return to the initial position and check for your opponent's simple threats. Never assume your move is safe without verification.
notes.plans: Black should have played Bh8, keeping the bishop and maintaining a winning position.

notes.explains: Blunders happen at all levels. The key is to learn from them and not be embarrassed. Even world champions have missed mate in one.
notes.teaches: When you blunder, analyze why it happened (e.g., tunnel vision, time pressure) and how to avoid it next time. Don't let embarrassment affect your play.

notes.explains: After the blunder, Black recovers and continues with a winning position. The bishop on e3 is a strong outpost, and Black has two extra pawns.
notes.teaches: After a blunder, stay calm and focus on the current position. Incremental improvements (like repositioning the rook to f8) can consolidate a win without unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Play Rf8, then consider Qf7 to create threats. Simple moves like Rcd8 also win by forcing rook trades.

notes.explains: Black's queen on f7 creates threats against the rook on e4 and the bishop on d3. The move Nb4 is strong, attacking c2 and threatening tactics.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for moves that create multiple threats. Qf7 opens an x-ray against the rook on e4, and Nb4 attacks c2, forcing concessions.
notes.plans: Play Nb4, threatening Nxc2. If White defends, Black can win material or deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf2, threatening mate on g2. White cannot defend adequately. Simpler moves like Rcd8 also win by forcing rook trades.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, choose the simplest winning continuation. Forcing rook trades reduces the chance of a blunder and is often the most efficient way to convert.
notes.plans: Play Qf2, threatening Qxg2#. If White checks, block with Rf7 and continue the attack.

notes.explains: Black's e5 is a blunder that loses a piece. White can capture with Nxe5 or Qxd4, both winning. Qxd4 is especially strong because it prevents queenside castling and threatens Qxa7.
notes.teaches: When you have a huge lead in development, look for direct tactical blows. A single mistake by the opponent can end the game immediately.
notes.plans: Capture on d4 with the queen, then play Bf4 to cover c7 and threaten checkmate on a8 or b8. Black's king is trapped.

notes.explains: Bf4 covers c7, threatening checkmate on a8 and b8. Black's king is trapped, and the only way to avoid immediate mate is to sacrifice the queen with Qd6.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces are active, look for mating nets. Covering escape squares is often more important than material.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, threatening Qa8# and Qb8#. If Black plays Qd6, capture it and win easily.

notes.explains: After …Nxd5 exd5 Qe7+ Qe2, Black's best is …Qxe2+ Bxe2. White has a slight edge due to better center control and the ability to damage Black's queenside pawn structure with Nxc6 or Bxc6.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a slight structural advantage (like damaged enemy pawns) can be a long-term asset. Choose captures that create weaknesses for the opponent.
notes.plans: White should aim to fix Black's queenside pawns on dark squares (e.g., a5) and then target them with the bishop and rooks.

notes.explains: After …d6 Bb5+ Bd7 Bxd7+ Qxd7 11.0-0 0-0 b3 a5 a4, White has fixed Black's a-pawn on a dark square, making it a permanent target. Black's bishop on c3 is annoying but White can play Bc4 and Rd3 to challenge it.
notes.teaches: Fixing an opponent's pawn on a square of your bishop's color creates a long-term weakness that can be attacked repeatedly. Use prophylactic moves like b3 and a4 to prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, then Rd3 to pressure the bishop on c3. If Black plays ...Be6, trade on e6 and then target the a5 pawn with Bd2.

notes.explains: White played Bc4 and Rd3, aiming to force Black's bishop away from c3. Black responded ...Bb6, and White continued Rd3, threatening Bxc6 and Rxc3 if Black captures on c4. This tactic wins a pawn if Black errs.
notes.teaches: When you have a tactical threat that wins material, pose it to the opponent even if it seems obvious. The psychological pressure can induce mistakes.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Bxc4, then Rxc3 wins the c6 pawn. If Black avoids the trade, continue improving piece placement.

notes.explains: After ...Bc3, White considered c3 to trap the bishop but rejected it because Black could play ...d5, opening a diagonal for the bishop. The correct idea was Kb3 or cxb4, leaving the bishop imprisoned. White missed this and played Kb2, allowing Black to escape.
notes.teaches: When a move like c3 would trap a piece, calculate deeply. Sometimes you can leave the piece imprisoned and play on with a material advantage elsewhere. Don't automatically assume the opponent can free it.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...d5, White can play cxb4, then Rxb4 and exploit Black's uncoordinated rooks. Alternatively, Kb3 prevents ...b3 and keeps the bishop trapped.

notes.explains: After ...Bd2, White traded bishops to simplify and target Black's queenside weaknesses. Then White played exd5 and c4, opening a second front. Black's position became untenable because his pieces were tied down to the a5 and c6 pawns.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage (e.g., fixed weaknesses), trade pieces that defend those weaknesses. Then open a second front to overload the opponent's defense.
notes.plans: Play exd5 first to avoid giving Black the f-file, then c4. If Black captures on c4, recapture with the rook and threaten Rd7.

notes.explains: White reached a rook endgame up a pawn with a 3 vs 2 on the kingside. The correct plan was to centralize the rook (Re4), bring the king up (Kc3), and then create a passed pawn on the kingside with f4-f5. White erred by playing h4 prematurely, allowing ...g5 and creating a weakness on g2.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, don't rush to create a passed pawn if it weakens your own pawns. First improve your king and rook, then advance pawns when the opponent's king is cut off.
notes.plans: Play Re4, then Kc3. If Black plays ...h5, answer with h4 to freeze the kingside. Then advance f4-f5 to create a passer.

notes.explains: White eventually created two passed pawns (a-pawn and f-pawn). The winning technique was to advance the king and pawn together, using the rook to cut off the enemy king. The Lucena position was not needed; simply zigzagging the king away from checks was sufficient.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with a passed pawn, advance your king in front of the pawn. Use the rook to block checks and cut off the enemy king. Avoid stepping onto squares where the rook can attack the pawn (e.g., f4).
notes.plans: Push the f-pawn to f7, then play Rf8 and Ke7. If the enemy king is on c7, use the Lucena method; otherwise, zigzag the king to safety.

notes.explains: After e4 d5 exd5 Nf6, the modern variation avoids the main line …Qxd5. White can play Bb5+ to force ...Bd7, which severs the queen's connection to d5 and leaves the bishop on d7 awkwardly placed.
notes.teaches: Forcing a piece to an awkward square can be worth more than winning a pawn. Here, Bb5+ develops with tempo and creates long-term positional pressure.
notes.plans: White intends to drop the bishop back to e2, give up the d5 pawn, and occupy the center with d4, aiming for a slight but safe advantage.

notes.explains: After Bb5+ Bd7 Be2, black often plays ...c5 to challenge the center. White can counter with c4, driving the knight back and establishing a strong pawn duo d4/c4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks your center, counter-attacking with a pawn push (c4) can be more effective than passive defense.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain the d4-c4 pawn chain, but must be ready to recapture with the d-pawn if black takes on d4.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...Nc6, White should immediately play c4 to challenge the knight on d5, rather than castling first. Delaying c4 allows Black to take on d4 and develop with ...Nc6, making c4 less effective.
notes.teaches: Meet central challenges directly; don't give the opponent time to complete development before striking.
notes.plans: After c4, if the knight moves, continue with Nc3 and development.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Nb4, White can simply play a3, chasing the knight. This is not dangerous because the bishop on e2 prevents the fork on c2.
notes.teaches: Don't fear knight jumps if you have a simple refutation; a3 gains time and space.
notes.plans: After a3, the knight retreats; continue developing with Nc3.

notes.explains: After …cxd5, White recaptures with the knight (Nxd5), not the queen, to avoid ...Nc6 attacking the queen. Keeping the queen centralized is less important than avoiding tempos.
notes.teaches: Recapture with the piece that doesn't walk into a developing move by the opponent.
notes.plans: After Nxd5, Black may play ...Nc6; White continues with development and prepares d5.

notes.explains: Now d5 is a strong tempo move, attacking the knight and preventing Black from playing ...Bd6 to blockade the passed pawn. The pawn becomes a powerful asset.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn is only strong if it cannot be blockaded; use tempo to deny the opponent the chance to blockade.
notes.plans: Follow with Bf4 to prevent ...Bd6, then continue development.

notes.explains: Bf4 prevents ...Bd6 and develops the bishop to an active square. If Black plays ...Bd6 anyway, the pawn on d5 supports Bf4, and the bishop is nearly trapped.
notes.teaches: Use your pawns to restrict the opponent's pieces; a passed pawn can also support your own pieces.
notes.plans: After Bf4, prepare to castle and bring the rook to d1.

notes.explains: After ...Bd6, White trades bishops, leaving Black with a weak dark-square complex and the passed pawn on d5 still strong. Black's queen on d6 is also exposed.
notes.teaches: Trading off a blockading piece can strengthen your passed pawn.
notes.plans: Castle, then bring the rook to d1 to pressure the queen and pawn.

notes.explains: Castling is better than playing a3 to kick the bishop on b4. a3 would take away the a3 square from White's dark-squared bishop, which could be a useful developing post if Black later takes on c3.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary pawn moves that might deprive your pieces of good squares; develop with maximum flexibility.
notes.plans: After castling, continue with Rad1 and consider Bg5 to pin the knight.

notes.explains: Bg5 pins the knight on f6, which is very dangerous for Black because the queen is also on the same diagonal. The threat of Nxg4 or d6 is strong.
notes.teaches: Pins are especially powerful when the pinned piece is defending the king or other important squares.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...h6, consider Bxf6 to open the g-file, or retreat to h4 to maintain the pin.

notes.explains: If Black weakens the kingside with ...g5, White retreats the bishop to g3, keeping the pressure. Black's pawn moves create permanent weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Provoke pawn weaknesses that compromise the opponent's king safety; the weaknesses will be exploitable later.
notes.plans: Continue with Rad1, preparing d6 or other breaks.

notes.explains: Rad1 is a crushing move: it threatens d6 (winning the bishop on d7) and also x-rays the queen. If Black plays ...Bc6, White can simply take on c7 because the queen on d4 is defended by the rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a simple rook move can create multiple threats. Concrete calculation must override general principles like 'connect pawns'.
notes.plans: After Rad1, Black is defenseless; White will win material by d6 or Bxf6.

notes.explains: Bxf6 is strong because after ...gxf6, the g-file opens, allowing Qd6–g3+ with a discovered check on the queen. The combination wins material.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a bishop to open a file can create a devastating discovered attack. Always look for ways to combine threats.
notes.plans: After ...gxf6, play Qg3+ to win the queen, then capture the rook.

notes.explains: Qg3+ is a discovered check that wins the queen on d8. The rook on d1 x-rays the queen, and the bishop on c6 cannot defend.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is on the same file as your rook, a discovered check can win it.
notes.plans: After the queen is captured, take the rook on c7 and then the bishop.

notes.explains: After Qg3+ Kh8, White captures the queen on d6, and the rook on c7 is now undefended. Next move, White wins the rook and then the bishop.
notes.teaches: A forced sequence of captures can win multiple pieces; always check if the opponent's pieces are left hanging.
notes.plans: Take the rook on c7, then the bishop on c6.

notes.explains: Nb5 attacks the rook on c7 and threatens Qg3+ again. The rook is overloaded, defending the bishop and the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's heavy pieces are tied to defense, a knight fork or discovered attack can decide the game.
notes.plans: If the rook moves, capture the bishop; if not, Nb5 wins the exchange.

notes.explains: Black's rook moves to c8, but White simply captures the bishop on c6, winning a piece. The combination is complete.
notes.teaches: After a successful combination, simplify to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Trade queens and win the endgame with an extra piece.

notes.explains: After some maneuvering, Black plays ...Rd8, a natural move to pressure d4. White's center is solid but Black aims to cause it to collapse.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld, the battle is over the center. Black tries to make White's center collapse, while White tries to expand and control key squares.
notes.plans: Black will look to open the c-file with ...cxd4 and then bring the rook to c8, pressuring the queen on c2. The bishop will go to e6, covering queenside squares.

notes.explains: White pushes d5, attacking the knight. Black retreats to b4, the only good square. The knight on b4 is awkward but necessary to avoid worse alternatives.
notes.teaches: When under attack, use process of elimination to find the least bad square. Sometimes a seemingly passive move is the only way to keep the position together.
notes.plans: Black will try to activate the knight later, perhaps via ...Nd3. Meanwhile, Black looks for tactical opportunities, such as exploiting the undefended bishop on b2.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a knight with …Nfxd5! The idea is to deflect the queen from defending the bishop on b2. After Nxd5 Bxd5, the queen has no safe square to maintain the defense of the bishop.
notes.teaches: When two enemy pieces are aligned and one is defended only by the queen, a sacrifice to deflect the queen can win material. Attacks on the queen are almost as powerful as checks.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, Black will regain the piece with interest, leaving Black up two pawns. The key is to follow up accurately, using intermediate moves like ...Nb6 to attack the queen again.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, Black plays …Nd3, attacking the queen and forcing it to abandon the bishop. Black emerges with two extra pawns.
notes.teaches: In tactical combinations, intermediate moves (like ...Nb6 and ...Nd3) are crucial to maximize gains. Always look for ways to keep the pressure on the opponent's queen.
notes.plans: Black is up two pawns but must consolidate. The king is vulnerable without the fianchetto bishop, so Black should aim to trade queens and simplify to an endgame.

notes.explains: After further complications, Black wins the exchange and remains up two pawns. However, White has active rooks and a vulnerable black king.
notes.teaches: Material advantage is not enough; you must also consider king safety and piece activity. Black must consolidate carefully.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade queens and bring the king to safety. The ideal setup is to centralize the king and rooks, then push the queenside majority.

notes.explains: Black's rook endgame technique: use the rook to attack weak pawns (like f2) and force White's rook to passive defense. Then create connected passed pawns on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king should be active. Use the rook to block lateral checks and advance pawns with the king's support.
notes.plans: Black will advance the kingside pawns (g4, h3, etc.) to create a passed pawn. The rook will block checks and the king will support the pawns.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo Attack (e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5), Black's choice between g6 and e6 depends on their repertoire against the Open Sicilian. For Accelerated Dragon players, g6 is natural and most popular.
notes.teaches: Your response to the Rossolimo should align with your Open Sicilian repertoire: e6 players often choose e6; Accelerated Dragon players should pick g6.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 4.0-0 Bg7 Re1, Black can play …e5. This move blocks the bishop and creates holes, but it strongly clamps down on d4 and prepares to develop the knight to e7.
notes.teaches: In closed Sicilian structures, e5 can be a powerful central clamp, preventing White's d4 break. The apparent weaknesses (blocked bishop, d5 hole) are manageable with proper piece coordination.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ne7, d6, and later consider f5 or kingside expansion.

notes.explains: After …e5, Black's knight goes to e7, and d6 solidifies the center. Delaying castling can be beneficial: if White plays Bg5, Black can respond with h6 and g5, keeping the king in the center or castling queenside for a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, delaying castling is a valid advanced technique. It allows flexible pawn advances on the kingside without exposing the king.
notes.plans: Consider h6, g5, and later g4 to attack White's kingside, especially if White has played h3.

notes.explains: In the position after …e5, c3 Ne7 d3 d6 Bg5, Black can play …f6. This weakens the a2-g8 diagonal but is safe because the center is closed. The follow-up Be6 covers the diagonal, and Black completes development.
notes.teaches: Moves like f6, which would be suicidal in open positions, become playable when the center is closed. Always compensate for weakened diagonals with proper piece placement.
notes.plans: Play Be6, then castle kingside, and prepare f5 to gain space on the kingside.

notes.explains: After …f6 Be3 Be6 Nbd2 0-0, Black's position is solid. White cannot play d4, and Black has no weaknesses. The knight on e7 and bishop on e6 defend d5. Black's plan is to slowly improve and eventually play f5.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, patience is key. Focus on incremental improvements and avoid rushing. A solid center with no weaknesses often gives Black a comfortable game.
notes.plans: Play f5 to gain space, then consider Bg4 to trade on f3 and occupy d4 with a knight.

notes.explains: The move Bg4 (after ...f5 preparation) aims to exchange on f3, ruining White's kingside pawn structure and planting a knight on d4. This creates threats like Qh3 and checkmate ideas, as White's knight on f3 has few retreat squares.
notes.teaches: Exchanging a bishop for a knight to damage the opponent's pawn structure is a classic idea, especially when the opponent's king is on that side. The resulting outpost for your knight can be decisive.
notes.plans: After Bg4 and exchanges, play Nd4, threatening forks and using the h3 square for the queen.

notes.explains: In the game, after …Bg4 Re3 Nd4, White's rook is awkward. If White retreats the knight to e1, Black can play f5, threatening f4 to trap the rook. The knight on e7 defends d5, allowing Black to ignore that square.
notes.teaches: When a piece has few retreat squares, target it with pawn advances. A trapped rook or knight can decide the game. Defensive pieces can be purely defensive and still valuable.
notes.plans: Play f5, then f4 to trap the rook, or if White avoids, continue with Be6 and queenside play.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, Black wins a piece for a pawn. The conversion is straightforward: activate the rook, centralize the queen, and use the extra material. White's rook on e3 is out of play.
notes.teaches: In won positions, simplify by trading down while maintaining activity. Avoid unnecessary risks; use your extra material to create threats.
notes.plans: Play Be6, Qb6, Rc8, and then push d5 or f5 to open lines.

notes.explains: After …O-O, White must avoid the center fork trick: if White castles, Black has Nxe4, Nxe4, d5 forking the knight and bishop. This would dissolve White's central advantage and free Black's light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is on c4 and the center is open, be alert to ...Nxe4 followed by ...d5. The simplest prophylaxis is to move the bishop to b3, keeping it on the active diagonal while defending e4 indirectly.
notes.plans: White can castle next, then prepare d4 or continue development. The bishop on b3 remains safe and maintains pressure on f7.

notes.explains: Black plays a6 preparing b5. White should prevent b5 with a4, because allowing b5 and then meeting it with a4 can lead to complications where Black pushes c5-c4, trapping the bishop. a4 is a direct prophylactic move that stops b5 immediately.
notes.teaches: When Black threatens queenside expansion with ...b5, a4 is often the cleanest way to stop it. Avoid inviting b5 unless you have a concrete follow-up that punishes it.
notes.plans: After a4, White castles and continues development. Black's light-squared bishop remains passive on d7.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to c6, creating tension on d4. White should not rush to trade or retreat; instead, play the improving move Re1, which is useful in many positions. Black then takes on d4, and White recaptures with the queen.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions with no immediate threats, play general improving moves like Re1. Avoid unnecessary trades when you have more space.
notes.plans: After Qxd4, White will decide where to place the bishop (f4 or g5) and continue central pressure.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on c6 is well-placed. White should avoid exchanging it because trades favor the side with less space. Instead, White plays Bf4, developing the bishop to a useful square even if it seems to 'bite on granite' (pawns block its diagonals). The bishop still supports central pressure and coordinates the rooks.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, avoid unnecessary trades. A bishop that appears passive can still be useful for prophylaxis and supporting central pawn breaks.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Qd2 to prevent ...Bf6 with tempo, then consider Nd5 to challenge Black's best piece.

notes.explains: Black defends d6 with Qc7, but White can improve with c3, creating a pawn bulwark that makes Black's bishop bite on granite. The bishop on b3 is undefended, but White should not fear one-move threats like Qb6; the bishop has retreat squares. This is a case where violating the principle of protecting pieces is acceptable because the threat is easily met.
notes.teaches: Do not fear one-move threats that can be parried easily. Sometimes you can leave a piece undefended if the opponent's counterplay is harmless.
notes.plans: White can play h3 to create luft, then consider f4 to push e5 and open lines. The backward d6 pawn remains a long-term target.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng6, attacking the bishop on f4, but this allows White to capture on d6 with tempo (attacking the rook on a8). White wins a pawn and now has a clear advantage. The weakness on d6, created earlier by Black's c6, is now exploited.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a backward pawn in the center, target it immediately. A central pawn weakness is much more serious than a flank weakness because its collapse often leads to a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: After taking on d6, White can push f4 to prepare e5, creating a devastating pawn chain. If Black takes on b2, White can trap the bishop with Kh1 and c3.

notes.explains: After winning the pawn, White pushes d7, threatening to promote. Black defends with Re7. White must find the winning move Qb4, which attacks the knight on f8 and prevents Black from defending the d7 pawn. The key is to induce ...Nf8 first, then Qb4 makes the threat of Qxf8 unstoppable.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a passed pawn, look for ways to attack the defender. Here Qb4 is a quiet move that ties Black's pieces to the defense of the knight, making promotion inevitable.
notes.plans: After Qb4, if Black plays c5, Qxc5 maintains the threat. If Black takes on d7, White recaptures with a new queen. The win is straightforward.

notes.explains: Black castles, walking into a classic Greek Gift sacrifice. White can play Bxh7+ followed by Ng5+, Qh5, etc., leading to a winning attack.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice is a standard attacking motif when the bishop is on d3 and the knight can reach g5. It exploits the weakened kingside after castling.
notes.plans: Execute Bxh7+ Kxh7, Ng5+ Kg6 (or Kg8), Qg4, etc., with a mating attack.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d4, and Black's bishop on c8 remains hemmed in. White has a small but lasting advantage due to superior piece activity and Black's bad bishop.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a bad bishop can be a decisive weakness. White should aim to keep the position closed and exploit Black's lack of space.
notes.plans: Play c3 to support the bishop, then develop the queenside with b3 and Bb2, gradually increasing pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the b2 pawn and preparing to support the queenside pawns. White should respond with a4 to break up Black's pawn chain.
notes.teaches: When Black builds a queenside pawn chain (b5, c4), White can undermine it with b3 and a4. The timing is critical: a4 is strong when the rook on a8 is undefended.
notes.plans: Play a4 immediately, exploiting the undefended rook on a8. If Black plays ...a6, then axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White plays a4, threatening to break the queenside pawn chain. Black cannot play ...a6 because axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend with a piece.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like a4 can be devastating when the opponent's rook is undefended. The threat of winning a pawn or exposing weaknesses forces concessions.
notes.plans: After a4, if Black plays ...Ba6, White can capture on b5 and c4, leaving Black with a weak pawn on c4. Then White will target that pawn with Rb1, Qe2, etc.

notes.explains: White clears the queenside pawns, leaving Black with a weak isolated pawn on c4. White now has a clear target and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Exchanging pawns to create a permanent weakness (isolated pawn) is a key strategic idea. The c4 pawn is a long-term liability for Black.
notes.plans: White will complete development (c3, Nbd2, Rc1, etc.) and then surround and win the c4 pawn. Black cannot easily defend it.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to solidify the center and prepares Nbd2 to target the c4 pawn. Black's rook on d8 does not threaten d4 because the knight on f3 guards it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, solidifying the center with c3 is often necessary before pursuing a queenside plan. The knight on f3 is a key defender.
notes.plans: White will play Nbd2, then perhaps Ne4 or Nf1-e3 to pressure c4. The c4 pawn is a fixed target that cannot be easily defended.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, challenging the e5 pawn and opening the center. White must reassess: the plan to target c4 is now secondary to exploiting the new weakness on e6.
notes.teaches: Flexibility is crucial. When the opponent changes the structure, be ready to switch plans. Here, the opening of the center favors the better-developed side (White).
notes.plans: White should capture on f6 (exf6), opening the e-file and targeting the weak e6 pawn. Then Qe2 or Rfe1 puts pressure on e6.

notes.explains: White captures on f6 and plays Rfe1, putting pressure on e6. Black's king is still in the center, and the e6 pawn is a major weakness.
notes.teaches: After opening the center, the side with better development should target the opponent's weak pawns. The rook on e1 adds pressure and prepares to double on the e-file.
notes.plans: White will play Qe2 or Qd3, attacking e6. Black cannot easily defend it because the king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf7 to defend e6, but this is a decisive mistake. White can now play Ng5+, forcing the king back or to a worse square.
notes.teaches: The king is a poor defender in open positions. Moving it forward often creates new tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: Play Ng5+ Ke7 (or Kg8), then capture on e6 with the rook or knight, winning a pawn and exposing the king further.

notes.explains: White plays d5, winning the knight on c6 because the queen on b6 is pinned to the king. Black's position collapses immediately.
notes.teaches: A pin can be decisive. Here, the queen's pin on the knight allows a simple pawn advance to win material and launch a mating attack.
notes.plans: After d5, Black cannot avoid losing the knight. White will then deliver checkmate with Qd4+ and Bf4, or similar.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qxd6#. The game is a clear example of converting a positional advantage into a direct attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped, a coordinated attack can end the game quickly. Accurate calculation of forcing moves is essential.
notes.plans: The mating sequence is forced: d5 wins the knight, then Qxd5+ forces the king to c7, and Bf4+ Bd6 Qxd6#.

notes.explains: This game illustrates key ideas of the Nimzowitsch French: rapid development, undermining the queenside pawn chain, flexibility in switching plans, and exploiting the opponent's king exposure.
notes.teaches: The Nimzowitsch French is a practical weapon that teaches closed position strategy, pawn breaks, and attacking chess. It is effective up to a high level.

notes.explains: White starts with Nc3 and Bf4, a setup that deliberately blocks the c-pawn to create fresh, imbalanced positions.
notes.teaches: In d4 openings, blocking the c-pawn usually violates the principle of controlling the center with c4, but here it's a calculated risk that leads to unique attacking chances.
notes.plans: White aims to develop quickly, often with ideas like Nb5 targeting c7, and later a kingside pawn storm with g4 and h4.

notes.explains: After Bf5, White can choose between the traditional f3 (preparing g4/h4) or the modern e3, aiming to quickly bring the knight to e5.
notes.teaches: The knight on e5 exerts strong pressure; Black often fails to see the threat of g4, which can trap the bishop or ruin Black's pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play e3, Nf3, then Ne5. If Black castles prematurely, g4 becomes very strong because the king is committed to the kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays Nbd7, which indirectly defends against g4. White should not play g4 here because after Bxe5 dxe5 Nxg4, White loses a pawn.
notes.teaches: When the knight on e5 is attacked, recapturing with the pawn can open lines, but here it's bad because Black's knight captures on g4 with tempo.
notes.plans: Instead of g4, develop the light-squared bishop to d3 or e2. Bd3 is more positional, preparing to recapture with the pawn after Bxd3, opening the c-file and giving the queen access to b3.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d3 with the pawn, accepting doubled pawns. This controls c4 and e4, opens the c-file for the rook, and allows the queen to go to b3.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness; here they control key central squares and create open lines for the heavy pieces.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qb3, Rc1, and later kingside expansion. The pawn on d3 is a strength, not a weakness.

notes.explains: Black plays c6, which is a blunder. White can win a pawn with Nxf7 (attacking the queen) followed by Nxd6, or even Nxc6 with further tactics.
notes.teaches: When the bishop on d6 is undefended, a discovered attack on the queen by the knight can win material. Always check for such tactical shots.
notes.plans: Play Nxf7, forcing the queen to move, then capture the bishop on d6. Alternatively, Nxc6 is also strong, threatening Nb5 after Qc7.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and has a comfortable position. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by improving your pieces and preventing counterplay. Don't rush; build up pressure gradually.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then consider f4 to reinforce the bishop on e5 and open lines for the rook. Also play b4 to stop c5, and a3 to defend the b-pawn.

notes.explains: White plays f4, reinforcing the bishop on e5 and preparing to lift the rook to f3 or g3. This also takes the sting out of ...Nxe5, as recapturing with the f-pawn opens the f-file.
notes.teaches: f4 is a useful multi-purpose move: it supports the bishop, prepares a rook lift, and can open the f-file for attack. The potential weakness of e3 is not a concern because Black cannot easily attack it.
notes.plans: Continue with Rf3, then double rooks on the f-file. Later, consider pushing f5 to open lines, but only after proper preparation.

notes.explains: White has built a strong position: the pawn on d3 controls key squares, the rooks are ready to double on the f-file, and Black is cramped. Black's Nd7 does not threaten anything immediately.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, improve your pieces without rushing. Here, White can bring the last rook to f1 to prepare for the f-file battle.
notes.plans: Play Rf1, then complete the rook lift to f3. Accumulate pressure on the kingside; Black will eventually crack under the strain.

notes.explains: White plays Bd6, chasing the rook from f8 and preparing f5. The bishop is safe here because it's hard to attack, and it can always return to e5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes retreating a piece to a seemingly passive square is actually strong because it prepares future advances and avoids being exchanged.
notes.plans: After Bd6, Black's rook must move (e.g., to e8). Then White can consider f5, opening the f-file. The bishop can later go back to e5 to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: White plays h3 to prevent ...Ng4 and then prepares to push g4, locking out Black's knight. This is a calm, positional approach rather than rushing with f5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a knight that could become active, it's often wise to restrict it with a pawn move like h3, then follow up with g4 to completely shut it out.
notes.plans: After h3, play g4, then consider e4 or f5. The rook on f3 can later go to g3 to target g7. Maintain control of all pawn breaks.

notes.explains: White plays e4, preventing ...Nf5 and keeping the g-file open for the rook. This is better than g4, which would block the rook on f3.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two good moves, consider which one leaves your pieces more active. Here, e4 keeps the rook's path to g3 open, while g4 would block it.
notes.plans: After e4, the rook can go to g3 to attack g7. The bishop on d6 can return to e5 to maintain pressure. White's position is very comfortable.

notes.explains: White returns the bishop to e5, where it pressures g7 and protects d4. Now ...d4 is no longer a threat, and Black's knight on h6 is out of play.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is to return a piece to its best square. The bishop on e5 is a monster, and White should not exchange it without good reason.
notes.plans: Now White can consider f5, which comes with tempo because it attacks the knight on g6. If Black takes on f5, White recaptures with the pawn and continues the attack.

notes.explains: Black exchanges on e5, and White recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file and giving White a powerful pawn center.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the pawn that opens a file for your rooks is often better than recapturing with a piece. Here, the f-file becomes a highway for White's attack.
notes.plans: Now White has a clear plan: double rooks on the f-file, then push f5 to break through. The pawn on e5 also restricts Black's pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh4, forking the rook on f3 and the pawn on f5. White responds with Rf4, defending the pawn and threatening to capture the knight.
notes.teaches: When your piece is forked, look for a move that defends the attacked piece and creates a counter-threat. Here, Rf4 both defends f5 and attacks the knight.
notes.plans: After Rf4, if Black takes on f5, White can play g4, trapping the knight. White's pieces are well-coordinated, and the attack continues.

notes.explains: Black plays Qg6, a tricky move that pins the g-pawn and threatens the rook on f4. White missed this and played Rxf5, but better was Rg3, keeping the pressure.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to pins and counterattacks. Here, Qg6 pins the g-pawn, so White cannot simply play gxf5. Instead, Rg3 would have avoided the pin and maintained the attack.
notes.plans: If White had played Rg3, the knight on f5 would be trapped, and White would win material. In the game, White played Rxf5, giving up the exchange but still winning due to the strong position.

notes.explains: White plays Kh2 to unpin the g-pawn and prepare to capture on f5. Now Black's queen is under attack, and White has a rook and two pieces for the queen.
notes.teaches: When your king is in a pin, moving it away can unlock your pieces. Here, Kh2 allows White to take on f5 and win material.
notes.plans: After Kh2, White will capture the queen with Rxf5, leaving White with a rook and bishop for the queen. The resulting position is winning due to Black's weak king and White's active pieces.

notes.explains: White plays Bg3, a quiet but strong move. It prepares to bring the bishop back to e5 later and avoids giving Black counterplay. The pawns will decide the game.
notes.teaches: In positions with a material advantage, it's important to consolidate and avoid unnecessary complications. Here, Bg3 is a flexible move that improves the bishop and prepares a pawn advance.
notes.plans: White will push the h-pawn to drive away Black's knight, then advance the g-pawn to open lines. The pawns are a decisive force.

notes.explains: White plays Nd2, aiming to bring the knight to f4 to join the attack. The knight has been idle and now becomes a key attacker.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, activate your worst piece. Here, the knight on c3 was doing nothing; bringing it to f4 increases the pressure on Black's king.
notes.plans: The knight will go to f4, then White can push g5 to open lines. The bishop on g3 can later go to h4 to target the rook on e7.

notes.explains: White plays Bh4, threatening to exchange on e7 or chase the rook. This improves the bishop and prepares g5.
notes.teaches: Even a small improvement like moving the bishop to a better diagonal can increase the pressure. Here, Bh4 eyes the rook on e7 and supports the g5 push.
notes.plans: After Bh4, White will play g5, opening lines. The knight on f4 and the pawns will decide the game.

notes.explains: White plays g5, opening lines and threatening g6. This is the decisive breakthrough.
notes.teaches: When you have accumulated enough pressure, it's time to open the position. Here, g5 is the right moment because White's pieces are optimally placed.
notes.plans: After g5, White will play g6, tearing open Black's kingside. The pawns and pieces will create a mating attack or win material.

notes.explains: White plays Qg5, attacking the knight on f6 and threatening h6. Black is forced to give up material.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for moves that create multiple threats. Here, Qg5 threatens h6 and also eyes the knight on f6, forcing Black to defend.
notes.plans: After Qg5, Black will have to move the knight or defend it. White will then play h6, breaking through. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange with Bxe7, leaving Black with a rook and knight against White's queen and bishop. The position is winning.
notes.teaches: In the attack, winning material is often as good as checkmate. Here, White simplifies to a technically winning endgame.
notes.plans: After Bxe7, White will consolidate and use the queen and bishop to target Black's weak king. The pawns will also be a factor.

notes.explains: White forces the win of a rook with Qg6+ and Qxe8+. Black's king is exposed, and White has a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, checks and threats can force the win of more material. Here, the queen's checks exploit Black's weak king position.
notes.plans: After Qxe8+, White will have queen and pawns against rook and knight. The win is a matter of technique.

notes.explains: White plays f4 before Nc3, which allows …d5. This is a legitimate but slightly inaccurate move order; the Grand Prix Attack usually starts with Nc3 to prevent d5.
notes.teaches: Punish inaccurate move orders by striking in the center immediately. …d5 challenges White's center and exploits the absence of the knight on c3.
notes.plans: After …d5, if White takes on d5, Black should not recapture with the queen but instead play Nf6, offering a pawn for rapid development and central control.

notes.explains: After exd5, Black plays …Nf6, not Qxd5. If White tries to hold the pawn with c4, Black plays e6, and after the trade on d5, Black gets tremendous positional compensation—better development and control of the center.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for rapid development and central control can be more valuable than material. The queen on d5 would be vulnerable without the knight on c3 to defend it.
notes.plans: Black will recapture the pawn on d5 later, enjoying a lead in development and pressure against White's center.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, threatening the knight on d5. Black should retreat the knight to b6, not take on f4. Taking on f4 would allow Qf3, creating awkward threats and blocking Black's dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: Don't grab pawns at the cost of piece activity and king safety. The pawn on f4 is actually beneficial for Black because it restricts White's bishop and king-side play.
notes.plans: Play Nb6, forcing the bishop to move. After Bb3, play c4, trapping the bishop and forcing Bb5+ (or Bc4). Then trade light-squared bishops with Bd7, simplifying into a favorable position.

notes.explains: Black forces the trade of light-squared bishops. White's dark-squared bishop is terrible because the pawn on f4 hems it in. Black gains control of the d4 square, a key outpost.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a bad bishop, trade the good one to leave them with the bad one. The c5 pawn controls d4, preventing White from playing d4 to free their position.
notes.plans: After the bishop trade, develop with Nc6, castles, and prepare to win back the pawn on d5. Black has a comfortable position with a clamp on d4.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, threatening Ng5 or Ne5. Black's priority is to get the king to safety and complete development. The long-term plan is 'castling by hand': move the king to g8 manually.
notes.teaches: When you cannot castle conventionally, you can manually castle by moving the king to g8 and the rook to f8 or e8. This is a common technique when the king has moved or the path is blocked.
notes.plans: Short-term: develop king-side pieces and avoid tactics. Long-term: play g6, Bg7, Rf8, and Kg8. The knight on f3 threatens e5, so Black must be careful not to allow a strong knight outpost.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, preparing Bg7 and manual castling. This is more important than developing the queen-side knight. White's attack is unsound; Black should not fear the exposed king.
notes.teaches: Prioritize king safety and development over material. Even if the king looks exposed, if the opponent lacks firepower, it is safe. Don't be intimidated by aggressive but unsound sacrifices.
notes.plans: Continue with Bg7, Rf8, Kg8. If White gives check on g5 or e5, Black can move the king to e8 or g8, and White's attack fizzles due to lack of pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Rf8, continuing manual castling. White now plays f5, trying to open lines. Black must decide how to recapture: with the pawn or with the bishop?
notes.teaches: When a pawn captures another pawn, consider which squares become newly accessible to the opponent. After gxf5, the h5 square becomes available to White's queen, which could lead to dangerous checks.
notes.plans: Black can take with the pawn (gxf5) or ignore the pawn and continue with Kg8. Taking with the pawn is principled but requires care against Qh5+ and Nf7 forks. Ignoring the pawn is also possible if Black calculates that White's attack is harmless.

notes.explains: Black takes on f5 with the pawn. Now White plays Ng5+ and Black must choose the correct king retreat. King to e8 would allow Qh5+ and a fork on f7. King to g8 is safer.
notes.teaches: In king safety, the square you retreat to matters. Avoid squares that allow the opponent to create double threats. Always consider checks and forks when moving the king.
notes.plans: After Kg8, if White plays Qh5, Black can defend f7 with Qf8. Then play h6 to drive the knight away. Black's king is safe and White's attack fizzles.

notes.explains: Black plays Kg8, avoiding the fork. White now plays Qh5, threatening Qxf7#. Black can defend with Qf8, then h6 to kick the knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent threatens mate, look for defensive moves that also counterattack. Qf8 defends f7 and prepares to trap the knight with h6.
notes.plans: Play Qf8, then h6. After the knight retreats, Black is safe and can complete development. Black is up a piece and will soon win the pawn on f5.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf8, defending f7 and preparing h6. White's attack is over. Black is up a piece and will soon consolidate.
notes.teaches: Once the immediate threats are parried, the defender's material advantage becomes decisive. Don't rush to counterattack; first ensure king safety.
notes.plans: Play h6, forcing the knight to move. Then recapture the pawn on f5 with the queen or bishop. Black will have a winning position.

notes.explains: Black plays h6, forcing the knight to retreat. White's attack is completely refuted. Black is up a piece and will soon win the pawn on f5.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to drive away attackers. Once the attacker is repelled, the defender's material advantage becomes decisive.
notes.plans: After the knight moves, play Qxf5 or Bxf5, then complete development with Nc6, etc. Black's king is safe and White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: White retreats the knight to f3. Black can now simply take the knight on f3, as White has no compensation. Alternatively, Black could play Qg4, trading queens, which is simplest.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplification is often the easiest path to victory. Trading queens reduces White's attacking chances and leaves Black with a decisive material advantage.
notes.plans: Play Qxf3 or Qg4 (forcing queen trade). Then develop the queen-side knight and rook. Black's king is safe and White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: Black takes the knight on f3. White has no attack left. Black is up a piece and will soon win the pawn on f5. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's attack is refuted, the defender should calmly capture material and consolidate. There is no need for risky counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Qxf5, then develop the queen-side. Black's king is safe and White's king is exposed. Black will soon launch a mating attack.

notes.explains: Black recaptures the pawn on f5. Now Black is up a piece and a pawn. White's king is exposed. Black should now look for a direct attack.
notes.teaches: Once material is secured, transition to a king hunt. The exposed white king is a target. Use checks and threats to force mate or win more material.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, then bring the rook to f8. Black can also consider Qd4+ to force the king to g2, then Qg4+ or other checks. The key is to calculate accurately to avoid counterplay.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to c6, preparing to bring the rook to f8. White's king is still on g1, vulnerable. Black should now consider checks like Qd4+.
notes.teaches: Keep your pieces active and coordinate them for an attack. The queen and rook can work together to exploit the exposed king.
notes.plans: Play Rf8, then Qd4+ to force the king to g2. Then Qg4+ or other checks. Black must calculate carefully to avoid letting White's king escape.

notes.explains: Black plays Rf8, activating the rook. White now plays Qh5, threatening Qxf7#. Black can defend with Qf8 again, but also has a tactical idea: Qd4+.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is on h5, the rook on f1 is undefended (type 2 undefended piece). A check on d4 can force the king to move, creating a discovered attack on the rook.
notes.plans: Play Qd4+! If Kg2, then Qg4+ forcing queen trade. If Kh1, then Bxe4+ wins. Black must calculate the line: Qd4+ Kg2 Qg4+ Kh1 Qxf5 Rxf5, and Black is up a piece.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd4+, forcing the king to g2. Now Black can play Qg4+, forcing queen trade. After Qxg4 hxg4, Black is up a piece and a pawn with a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, trading queens simplifies the position and reduces counterplay. The check on d4 also exploits the undefended rook on f1.
notes.plans: After Qg4+, White must trade queens. Then Black has a winning endgame. Alternatively, Black could play for mate, but simplification is safer.

notes.explains: Black plays Qg4+, forcing queen trade. White cannot avoid it without losing material. After the trade, Black is up a piece and a pawn.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, the simplest path is often the best. Forcing a queen trade removes all counterplay and leaves you with a technically winning endgame.
notes.plans: After Qxg4 hxg4, Black has a rook and knight for a rook and pawn, with an extra piece. Develop the queen-side and push pawns.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black is up a piece and a pawn. The endgame is winning. Black should develop the queen-side and activate the king.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, activate your king and centralize your pieces. Avoid unnecessary risks and use your material advantage to create passed pawns.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, then bring the rook to f8. The king can go to g7 or h7. Push the queen-side pawns. White has no counterplay.

notes.explains: After both kings move to b1 and b8, White's next step is to trade off Black's strongest piece: the bishop on e5. Bf4 is a good move because it exchanges a powerful bishop for a passive one, and the tactics work (Nxd4 is impossible due to pin).
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's best piece is a key positional idea. Here, the bishop on e5 controls many squares; removing it leaves Black with a bad bishop on e6.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, then after the trade, bring the rook to e1 to pressure the e6 bishop, and continue improving pieces.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade, White has a pleasant position. The next step is to bring the rook to e1, putting pressure on the e6 bishop. Black's pieces are passive, and White can continue accumulating pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, keep making improving moves. Bring rooks to open files, target weak pieces, and avoid rushing. The opponent will eventually run out of good moves.
notes.plans: Play Rde1, then consider tactical ideas like Bxe6 followed by Qd6 trade, exploiting the alignment of rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd6, offering a queen trade. White can transform the positional advantage into a tactical one by noticing the alignment of rooks on the d-file and the undefended rook on d6. The sequence Bxe6 (defending the queen), then Qxd6, then Nxe6 exploits this.
notes.teaches: When all your pieces are on perfect squares, look for tactics. Here, the undefended rook on d6 and the alignment of heavy pieces create a tactical opportunity. Don't be afraid to change the pawn structure to shift the target of attack.
notes.plans: Play Bxe6, then Qxd6, then Nxe6, winning a pawn. The resulting endgame is winning due to the weak e6 pawn and active pieces.

notes.explains: After Nxe6, White has won a pawn. The knight on e6 is strong, controlling d8 and attacking the d5 pawn. Black's pieces are passive. White's plan is to consolidate and win more pawns.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, keep your rooks on open files and use your knight to create threats. Avoid tunneling on one weakness; look for ways to create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Play Ba4 (to later go to b3, attacking d5), then c3 to immobilize d5, and eventually win the d5 pawn. If Black tries counterplay, use tactics like Ng7 to fork rooks.

notes.explains: After …Nb4, White has a winning tactic: Ng7 forks the rooks. This move is easy to miss because the knight goes to an unusual square (g7), but it exploits the undefended rook on e8 and the pinned knight on e7.
notes.teaches: Avoid tunnel vision on one plan (e.g., winning the d5 pawn). Look for geometric moves like knight forks. When your pieces are well-placed, always check for tactical blows that win material immediately.
notes.plans: Play Ng7, winning the exchange. After that, use the extra material to win the game.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 and pressures e4. White's Bd3 develops and defends e4, neutralizing the pin.
notes.teaches: Against early ...Bb4 in Owen's Defense, develop Bd3 to defend e4 and prepare to break the pin without wasting time on a3.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ne2 to connect knights and prepare to castle kingside, ignoring the bishop on b4.

notes.explains: Black voluntarily gives up the bishop pair by capturing on c3, which is a positional mistake. White recaptures with the b-pawn, keeping the e4 pawn defended and gaining the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading your bishop for a knight without compensation, especially when you have the bishop pair. White's doubled c-pawns are not a weakness here because they control central squares.
notes.plans: Continue development with Ne2, castle kingside, and prepare e5 to gain space and attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays h6 to prevent Bg5, which would pin the knight and create kingside weaknesses. White now has a choice between developing or expanding.
notes.teaches: When the opponent prevents a pin, consider whether to switch to a different plan. Here, expanding with e5 is more ambitious than routine development.
notes.plans: Play e5 to gain space and prepare Qg4, targeting the weak g7 pawn and exploiting Black's lack of kingside development.

notes.explains: White plays Qg4, threatening the g7 pawn and forcing Black to weaken the kingside. Black cannot castle because of the pin on h6, and g6 creates a hole on f6.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's kingside is undeveloped, a queen sortie to g4 can create decisive threats. The weakness of g7 is a common target in such positions.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ne4, c4 to chase the knight from d5, and then Nf6+ if possible. If Black plays g6, the f6 hole becomes a permanent weakness.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, further weakening the kingside. White can now open the f-file with f4, exploiting the pawn on g5 as a hook.
notes.teaches: A pawn like g5 can be used as a hook to open lines for an attack. f4 is a typical break to open the f-file against an uncastled king.
notes.plans: Play f4, and if ...gxf4, recapture with the bishop and then target g7 with Qg7. If ...Nxf4, consider taking on d5 first to prevent counterplay.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the bishop on f4, maintaining pressure. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White threatens Qg7, winning the rook on h8.
notes.teaches: After opening the f-file, the rook on f1 and queen on g4 combine to create mating threats. The bishop on f4 also eyes h6, adding to the attack.
notes.plans: Play Qg7, forcing ...Rf8, then Bxh6, breaking through. If Black defends with ...Qe7, consider Ne4 or other consolidating moves.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, ignoring the kingside threat, and White opens the g-file with g6. This exploits Black's lack of development and exposes the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent ignores your attack, punish them by opening more lines. g6 is a typical pawn sacrifice to open the g-file and accelerate the attack.
notes.plans: Recapture on g6 with the queen or rook, then double rooks on the g-file and bring the bishop to f4 or e5 to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays Rf7, skewering the king and the bishop on b7. The rook on the seventh rank is devastating, as it attacks everything on that rank.
notes.teaches: An open file allows the rook to penetrate to the seventh rank, where it can create decisive threats. Rf7 is a natural move that cannot be bad.
notes.plans: Continue with simple captures and checks, such as Nxd5 or exd6, to win material while maintaining the attack. Do not overcomplicate.

notes.explains: White plays Be5, defending the d4 pawn with tempo and cutting off the king's escape squares. Now White threatens b3 followed by c4#.
notes.teaches: When the king is trapped, look for mating constructions. Be5 is a quiet move that sets up a deadly pawn mate, demonstrating the power of restricting the king.
notes.plans: Play b3, threatening c4#. If Black plays ...Rxg6, then Re1 deprives the king of e4, and c4 is mate. If Black plays ...Nc6, then Rd7#.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Rd7#, exploiting the pin on the knight and the king's lack of escape squares.
notes.teaches: After restricting the king, a simple rook check can be mate. Always consider all legal moves of the opponent to ensure no hidden defenses exist.

notes.explains: Black plays ...d5, transposing to a French-like structure. White must be careful because ...c5 is a serious threat, as there is no c3 pawn to defend the chain.
notes.teaches: In this line, after e5, Black's ...c5 can be dangerous because White cannot play c3. White must respond actively, typically with Nf4 or a tactical shot.
notes.plans: Play Nf4, and if ...c5, then Nxc6! forcing ...dxc6, then Qh5+ g6, Bxg6+ Ke7, and Bg5+ winning. This line exploits Black's weak dark squares.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a knight to open lines and deliver a devastating checkmate attack. The key is the bishop on g5 check, forcing ...Nf6, then exf6+ and Bxf6+ Kxf6, followed by a skewer.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for sacrificial combinations to open lines. The skewer at the end (Bg5+ ...Kxf6, then Qg5+? no, actually after Bxf6+ Kxf6, Qh4+ wins the queen) is a common tactical motif.
notes.plans: After Bg5+, if ...Nf6, then exf6+ Kxf6, and Qh4+ winning the queen. If ...Ke8, then Qxg6+ hxg6, Bxg6#.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White wins the queen with Qh4+, as the king is forced to move and the queen is lost.
notes.teaches: Always check for checks and captures at the end of a combination. Here, Qh4+ is a double attack that wins the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ne4, a typical idea in the Caro-Kann. White must respond with the counterintuitive Nb1, preparing to trap the knight with f3.
notes.teaches: When a knight jumps to e4, the idea of retreating the knight to b1 to play f3 is a known concept. This prevents the knight from escaping via ...Nxc3 and allows White to trap it.
notes.plans: Play Nb1, then if Black plays ...c5, play c3 to solidify the center. Then f3 wins the knight. If Black plays ...Bg4, then f3 still wins.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to prevent ...c4 and then f3 traps the knight on e4. Black's knight is stranded and will be lost.
