notes.plans: Black continues with ...a4, then ...Rxa4? is not forced; instead, after ...a4 b4, Black can play ...Nb4 or ...Qb6, targeting the weak d3 pawn. White should play Rb1 to keep the queenside closed.

notes.explains: Black plays …a4, opening the a-file. White's bxa4? would allow …Rxa4, and the rook is active. Instead, White played 31.F4?, a blunder that loses a rook because the rook on f1 is undefended: …Bxf4 gxf4 Rxf4, and the rook on f1 is hanging. The correct move was Rb1, keeping the queenside closed.
notes.teaches: When under pressure, avoid panicking with weakening pawn moves like f4. Instead, look for prophylactic moves that maintain the status quo.
notes.plans: After …Bxf4, Black is up a rook. The game is effectively over; Black should simplify by trading pieces and converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: After trading queens, Black has a rook and bishop vs rook and bishop endgame with an extra pawn. The a-pawn is a dangerous passed pawn. Black's plan is to advance it, supported by the rook from behind.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a passed pawn supported by a rook from behind is very strong. The king can also help escort the pawn.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rc2 to attack the a2 pawn, win it, and then push the a-pawn. White's rook is tied to defense.

notes.explains: Black plays ...h5 to gain space on the kingside and create a favorable pawn structure (f7, g6, h5). This makes it harder for White to attack the pawns and prepares future king activity.
notes.teaches: In endgames, arranging pawns so they are not on the same rank (e.g., f7, g6, h5) makes them harder to capture by a rook. This is a small but important detail.
notes.plans: Black will continue to improve piece placement, eventually pushing the a-pawn. The king can later march to the center.

notes.explains: Black plays ...b6 to protect the b7 pawn, freeing the rook to move. This is a prophylactic move that eliminates any back-rank threats and allows the rook to be more active.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis is important: anticipate opponent's threats and neutralize them before they become serious. ...b6 is a simple way to secure the pawn and avoid tactics.
notes.plans: Black will now aim to double rooks on the c-file or push the a-pawn. The rook on c2 is well placed.

notes.explains: Black trades queens and then plays ...Rc2, attacking the a2 pawn. White cannot defend it easily. Black will win the pawn and promote the a-pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, an active rook on the second rank can be devastating. The a-pawn becomes a decisive passed pawn.
notes.plans: Black will capture on a2, then push the a-pawn. White's rook is tied to defense, and Black's king can assist.

notes.explains: Black wins the a2 pawn. Now Black has a passed a-pawn and a rook on the second rank. White's rook is passive.
notes.teaches: Once a passed pawn is created, advance it with the support of the rook. The king can also help by moving toward the pawn.
notes.plans: Black will push the a-pawn, using the rook to support it from behind. White's rook cannot stop it alone.

notes.explains: Black pushes the a-pawn. White's rook on b1 tries to block, but the pawn is unstoppable. Black's rook on a2 supports the advance.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn supported by a rook from behind is a decisive advantage. The opponent's rook cannot effectively block if the pawn is far advanced.
notes.plans: Black will continue pushing the a-pawn. If White's rook blocks, Black can trade rooks or use the king to assist.

notes.explains: Black's a-pawn advances to a4. White's rook on b4 tries to stop it, but Black can play ...Bb2 to cut off the rook's connection to the pawn, or simply push further.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, using the bishop to intercept the rook's defense of a square can be a decisive tactic. The bishop on b2 ties White's rook to the back rank.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Bb2, forcing White's rook to move, then push the pawn. Alternatively, Black can simply push the pawn and trade rooks if possible.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bb2, cutting off the rook's defense of the a-pawn. White's rook cannot stop the pawn from promoting. This is a winning tactic.
notes.teaches: A bishop can be used to intercept the opponent's rook's line of defense, creating a decisive passed pawn. This is a common endgame motif.
notes.plans: Black will push the a-pawn to promotion. White's rook is helpless.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the exchange to stop the pawn, but Black recaptures and the a-pawn is still unstoppable. Black's rook and king will support the pawn.
notes.teaches: Even if the opponent sacrifices material to stop a passed pawn, the pawn can still be decisive if it is far advanced and supported.
notes.plans: Black will push the a-pawn to promotion. White's rook alone cannot stop it.

notes.explains: Black promotes the a-pawn to a queen. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn supported by a rook and king is a decisive advantage. The conversion is straightforward once the pawn reaches the seventh rank.
notes.plans: Black will use the queen to win more material or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: After Bd3 d6, White repositions the bishop to b5, pinning the knight and threatening to recapture the d4-pawn with interest. This is a key idea in the modern treatment of the Belgrade.
notes.teaches: Repositioning a piece to a more active diagonal can create new threats and improve coordination. The bishop on b5 pins the knight and eyes the d4-pawn.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Nxd4, recovering the pawn and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne5, offering a second knight and threatening the Noah's Ark trap (c5-c4 trapping the bishop). White must avoid taking on e5 and instead play Nxd4, which is the critical response.
notes.teaches: The Noah's Ark trap is a classic pattern where pawn advances trap a bishop. When facing such threats, look for tactical resources to save the piece, often involving counterattacks.
notes.plans: White plays Nxd4, and if c5, then Nxf6+ followed by Bd5, attacking the rook on h8 and creating counterplay.

notes.explains: After Bd5, White attacks the rook on h8 and threatens to win the exchange. Black's best response is cxd4, leading to a complex tactical sequence where White must find the only moves to maintain the balance.
notes.teaches: In sharp tactical positions, prioritize concrete calculation over general principles. Look for forcing moves that create threats and limit the opponent's options.
notes.plans: After cxd4, White should play Qd2 (not Qxd4, which loses to Bg4 and Nf3+), preparing to meet Bg4 with Qd2 and consolidating the extra exchange.

notes.explains: Black played Bg4 immediately, allowing White to save the knight with Ne2. This is a mistake; Black should have played cxd4 first, leading to the Bd5 line. Now White is clearly better.
notes.teaches: When you have a tactical resource, execute it in the correct order. Playing Bg4 before cxd4 allows White to avoid the complications and keep a material advantage.
notes.plans: White will castle, then play f3 to chase the bishop, and eventually bring the knight to d5 via f4 or c3.

notes.explains: After …Qc6, White played Nf4, which is best. Black's queen is forced to c6, the only square that maintains the balance. Other squares like d6 or b6 allow White to gain a decisive advantage.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, the opponent's queen is often a target. Forcing it to a less active square can limit counterplay and prepare a decisive attack.
notes.plans: White should now play Rfe1, preventing Black from castling and maintaining pressure. The immediate Nf4 is strong, but White must be careful not to allow Black to consolidate.

notes.explains: White played Rfe1, a natural move that is actually a mistake. Black can respond with Nf6, restricting the knight on f4 and preparing to castle. The correct move was Nf5, immediately threatening to win material.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, don't waste time on slow moves. Look for the most forcing continuation to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: White should have played Nf5, threatening Nxg7 and forcing Black to defend. After Rfe1, Black can play Nf6 and then Rb7, preparing to castle and neutralize White's attack.

notes.explains: Black played Nf6, restricting the knight on f4 and threatening to castle. White now must find a way to prevent Black from castling. The best move is Qf3, which sets up threats against f7 and prepares to meet ...Qd4+ with Kh1.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, every tempo counts. Preventing castling is often worth a pawn sacrifice.
notes.plans: White plays Qf3, threatening Qxf7+ and also preparing Rfe1 to keep the king in the center. Black's best response is Rc8, defending the bishop and preparing to castle.

notes.explains: Black played Rc8, defending the bishop and preparing to castle. White now has a choice: Bf4, bringing the bishop into the attack, or Qf3, which was played. Qf3 is a mistake because it allows ...Nd7-e5, hitting the queen and defending. The correct move was Bf4.
notes.teaches: When attacking, bring all your pieces into the game. Bf4 develops with tempo and threatens Bxc7, while Qf3 puts the queen on a vulnerable square.
notes.plans: White should play Bf4, then after Rc8, Qe1 and Rd1, maintaining pressure. Black's best defense is ...Nd7, preparing ...Ne5 to block the attack.

notes.explains: Black played Bf6, a strong move that defends the queen and prepares to castle. White now played Bf4, which is correct. The position is complex, but White has compensation for the pawn.
notes.teaches: In dynamic positions, bishops can be powerful defenders. Bf6 covers key squares and prepares to complete development.
notes.plans: White should continue with Qe1 or Rd1, maintaining pressure. Black's king is still in the center, and White can try to open lines with e5 or f5.

notes.explains: After …Nf6, White played c3, a slow move that aims to trap the bishop on f6. This is a practical decision in time pressure, but the engine prefers more direct moves like Rxb2 or e5.
notes.teaches: In time trouble, it's often better to play simple, solid moves that maintain the pressure rather than forcing lines that require precise calculation.
notes.plans: White plans to play c3, then eventually recover the pawn on d4 or create threats against Black's king. Black must be careful not to allow White to consolidate.

notes.explains: After Bxc7, Black has a choice. The best move is Rd1, which sets up a mating threat (Bxd1? Qa8#) and forces White to find a perpetual check. Instead, Black played Rc8, a blunder that loses to Bxd6.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, always be alert to tactical threats. Rd1 is a strong resource that creates counterplay and should not be underestimated.
notes.plans: White should play Bxd6, winning a piece. Black's only chance is to create counterplay, but White's material advantage should decide.

notes.explains: After Bxd6, White is winning. Black's rook on c8 is attacked, and White has a decisive material advantage. The game ends shortly.
notes.teaches: Converting a material advantage in the endgame requires accuracy. Avoid unnecessary risks and simplify when possible.
notes.plans: White will capture the rook on c8 and then promote the pawn or use the extra piece to win.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5, the Rossolimo is a positional alternative to the Open Sicilian. Black can choose between …g6 (for Accelerated Dragon players) or …e6 (for Taimanov/Paulsen players).
notes.teaches: Choose your response to the Rossolimo based on your main Sicilian repertoire. The move g6 is consistent for Accelerated Dragon players.
notes.plans: Black aims to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and later clamp down on the d4 square with ...e5.

notes.explains: After …g6 Bxc6, Black should recapture with the d-pawn (…dxc6) rather than the bishop. This opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop and gives the queen access to the d-file, increasing central control.
notes.teaches: Capture away from the center when it opens lines for your pieces and improves central influence.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g7, then aim for ...e5 to clamp down on d4.

notes.explains: After ...dxc6, ...Bg7, and ...Nf6, White often plays h3 to prevent ...Bg4. Black can still play ...Bg4 anyway, trading the bishop for the knight to reduce White's control and then drop the knight back to d7.
notes.teaches: Trading a bishop for a knight can be a positional decision to relieve pressure and prepare a central pawn push.
notes.plans: Play ...Bg4, ...Bxf3, then ...Nd7, followed by ...e5 to solidify the center.

notes.explains: The knight on d7 is flexible: it can go to f8, then e6, and eventually d4, targeting the outpost. Overprotecting the e5 pawn with ...Re8 frees the knight to maneuver.
notes.teaches: Overprotection (Nimzowitsch) allows a piece to leave its defensive duty because the pawn is already sufficiently guarded.
notes.plans: Maneuver the knight from d7 to f8, then e6, and finally d4, using the rook on e8 to cover e5.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+, Black has three main replies: Qd7 (dubious but sharp), Bd7 (solid but drawish), and Nd7 (the choice of most top players aiming for a win). Nd7 strikes a balance between sharpness and soundness.
notes.teaches: When choosing a response in the opening, consider the trade-off between solidity and winning chances. The most popular move among strong players often offers the best practical balance.
notes.plans: Black will develop naturally, aiming for a Scheveningen-like structure with e6 and d6, and wait for White to commit to d4.

notes.explains: White retreats the knight to c2 after capturing on d7. This avoids the trap Qe8 and keeps a stable advantage. The knight will reroute to e3 to pressure d5 and f5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a retreat is necessary to maintain a safe advantage. The knight on c2 can later go to e3, targeting the weak d5 and f5 squares.
notes.plans: Play Qf3 to attack f6 and d5, then Ne3 to threaten Nf5 with mating ideas. Combine pressure on the weak pawns with king safety threats.

notes.explains: White's queen moves to g5, forking the king and the d5 pawn. Black's position collapses due to multiple weaknesses: the d5 pawn, the f6 pawn, and the exposed king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has multiple weaknesses, combine threats. A queen fork or a knight fork can win material. Patiently bring all pieces to the attack before striking.
notes.plans: Capture the d5 pawn, then trade queens and convert the extra pawn in the endgame. Avoid rushing; slow, improving moves are often best when the opponent has no counterplay.

notes.explains: Bc4 is a common beginner move against the Sicilian, but e6 blunts the bishop's diagonal and prepares d5 with tempo.
notes.teaches: Against Bc4 in the Sicilian, e6 is a principled response that immediately challenges the bishop's placement.
notes.plans: Follow up with d5 to gain space and tempo, or develop normally with Nf6 and Be7.

notes.explains: After c3 (preparing d4), d5 strikes in the center with tempo, forcing an exchange that opens the position favorably for Black.
notes.teaches: When White plays c3 in the Sicilian, d5 is a strong central break that exploits the bishop's awkward position.
notes.plans: After exd5 exd5, develop naturally: Nf6, Be7, O-O, and later consider c4 or other breaks.

notes.explains: With the bishop on b3, Black should develop the knight to f6 (not e7, which blocks the dark-squared bishop).
notes.teaches: Develop knights before bishops in most positions, and avoid blocking your own pieces.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then Be7 or Bd6, O-O, and later develop the light-squared bishop to g4 or f5.

notes.explains: c4 is a weakening move that creates a backward d2-pawn. Black can take on c4 or push d4; taking on c4 leaves White with a structural weakness.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens their pawn structure, consider capturing to leave them with a long-term liability.
notes.plans: After dxc4 Bxc4, develop Bd6 (exploiting that d4 is not playable due to Bxh2+), then O-O and pressure d2.

notes.explains: Bd6 is active and prevents d4 because of the tactical motif Bxh2+ winning the queen after Kxh2 Ng4+.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on active squares when the opponent cannot challenge them due to tactical threats.
notes.plans: O-O, then develop the light-squared bishop to g4, aiming for Nd4 and Bxf3 to ruin White's kingside pawns.

notes.explains: h6 prevents Bg5, which could pin the knight. This prophylactic move is useful when the opponent has no immediate threats.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis: prevent your opponent's best moves even if they seem harmless; it limits their options.
notes.plans: After h6, develop Bg4, pinning the knight and threatening Nd4 followed by Bxf3.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White cannot easily break the pin because Be2 is unavailable (pawn on d3 blocks). The threat is Nd4, forcing Bxf3 and ruining White's kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: A pin is powerful when the opponent cannot unravel it; combine it with threats like Nd4 to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, threatening Bxf3. After gxf3, Black's dark-squared bishop targets h2, and the queen can join via h4 or h3.

notes.explains: Nd4 threatens Bxf3. White's queen on b3 does not defend f3 adequately; after Bxf3 gxf3, Black's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pinned knight, a knight jump to a central square can force a favorable exchange that destroys the opponent's pawn cover.
notes.plans: After Bxf3 gxf3, bring the queen to h4 or h3, and use the dark-squared bishop to target h2.

notes.explains: White blunders with Bxf7+, allowing a forced sequence that wins material and exposes the king. Black's attack is decisive.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for forcing sequences that remove defenders and expose the enemy king.
notes.plans: After Bxh2+, Kxh2 Qh4+ and mate follows.

notes.explains: If White retreats the queen to d1, Black should avoid Qd7? (allows Kg2) and instead play Nh5, threatening Qh4. After g4, Qh4! is strong because the bishop cannot take (knight on h5 controls f4).
notes.teaches: In attack, bring the queen to the kingside via h4 or h3. Use knight maneuvers to control key squares like f4.
notes.plans: After Nh5 g4, Qh4 threatens Nxf3+ and mate. White must play Bd5, then Black lifts the rook to g6.

notes.explains: Black's attack is unstoppable; the queen on f4 threatens mate and the knight on h5 supports further threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, coordinate your queen and minor pieces to create multiple mating threats.
notes.plans: Continue with Rfe8 or Nxf4, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Instead of d5, Nf6 is also playable. White's best is d4, but after cxd4 cxd4, Black can play d5 with tempo, or allow the center fork trick.
notes.teaches: There are multiple good moves; choose based on your style. Nf6 leads to more tactical play.
notes.plans: After d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5, Black equalizes. Alternatively, if White plays e5, Ng4 and later d6.

notes.explains: Black plays the center fork trick: Nxe4, sacrificing a knight to fork White's bishop and knight with d5. White's a3 move makes this even stronger.
notes.teaches: The center fork trick (Nxe4 followed by d5) is a key tactical motif when a bishop is on c4 (or c5 for Black). It wins back the piece with interest.
notes.plans: After d5, Black regains the piece and White's king is stuck in the center.

notes.explains: d3 avoids the center fork trick but allows d5, transposing to similar positions.
notes.teaches: If White avoids the trick, Black can still play d5 and develop normally.
notes.plans: After …d5, trade on d5 and develop with Be7, O-O, etc.

notes.explains: Nc3 defends e4 but allows the center fork trick in an improved form: …Nxe4? Nxe4 d5, and Black wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: When a knight defends e4, the center fork trick still works if the knight can be captured.
notes.plans: After …d5, Black wins a pawn or gets a strong initiative.

notes.explains: e5 forces Ng4, then Black plays d6 to break the center.
notes.teaches: When pushed by e5, counter in the center with d6 to undermine the pawn chain.
notes.plans: After …Ng4 Re1 d6, Black gets good piece play.

notes.explains: d4 is principled. After cxd4 cxd4, Black can play d5 or Nxe4. The trick is …Nxe4? d5!? Actually, …d5 is solid.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, d4 is the main break; Black must be ready to counter.
notes.plans: After …cxd4 cxd4 d5, Black equalizes. If …Nxe4, White can play d5! with complications.

notes.explains: A tactical line where Black wins a pawn but White gets compensation. Black should be careful.
notes.teaches: Tactical lines require precise calculation; sometimes it's better to avoid complications.
notes.plans: Black is a pawn up but White has development; play solidly.

notes.explains: The London System is a solid but passive setup for White; Black's most combative response is c5, immediately challenging White's center and aiming for an unbalanced, dynamic game.
notes.teaches: Against the London, choose a system you know well; c5 leads to imbalanced positions that can make London players uncomfortable.
notes.plans: After c5, if White plays e3, Black can play d5 transposing to main lines, or deviate with an early Qb6 to pressure b2 and d4.

notes.explains: After cxd4, Black's queen on b6 pressures both b2 and d4, exploiting the early bishop development which leaves b2 undefended.
notes.teaches: The queen on b6 is a typical London counter: it pressures two pawns and forces White to make positional concessions to defend.
notes.plans: Black aims to maintain pressure on d4 while developing; White's common defensive moves like b3 weaken dark squares.

notes.explains: White's Nc3 is principled but allows Black to choose among several setups; the move a6 is underrated and leads to unexplored positions.
notes.teaches: When facing Nc3, Black can play a6 to cover b5, preparing d5 and avoiding the Jobava London knight maneuver to b5.
notes.plans: After a6, Black plays d5, contesting the center and creating a structure similar to the Exchange Caro-Kann, with a comfortable game.

notes.explains: White's Rb1 defends b2 without weakening dark squares, but Black's d5 creates a solid center and prepares development.
notes.teaches: After Rb1, Black can play d5 confidently; the resulting pawn structure is favorable for Black, resembling an Exchange Caro-Kann where Black has no weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will develop naturally with e6, Bd6, Nc6, and castle, aiming for a comfortable middlegame with pressure on d4.

notes.explains: White's Nf3 is a natural move but a positional inaccuracy because it allows Bg4, which pressures the d4 pawn by targeting its defender.
notes.teaches: When White has a knight on c3 instead of c3 pawn, the d4 pawn becomes a weakness; Bg4 exploits this by threatening to exchange the knight that defends d4.
notes.plans: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight and increasing pressure on d4; if White plays Ne5, Black exchanges on e2 and recaptures with the knight to keep c3 available.

notes.explains: White's Be3 is a retreat that overprotects d4 but loses time; Black can now develop freely without fear of Ne5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent retreats, don't rush to exchange; continue developing and maintain the tension. The bishop pair is valuable, so avoid giving it up without reason.
notes.plans: Black plays e6, reinforcing the center and preparing Bd6; the bishop on h5 keeps pressure on the knight, and Black will castle and aim for a slow squeeze.

notes.explains: Black's b5 grabs space on the queenside, making it harder for White to find active play. White's position is already passive.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, use it to restrict the opponent's pieces. Moves like b5 are 'low-hanging fruit' that improve your position without needing a concrete plan.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Rc8 or Bb7, preparing to double rooks on the c-file or target the c2 pawn. The knight can later maneuver to c4 via b8-d7-b6.

notes.explains: White's b4 is a panic move that weakens the queenside and leaves the knight on c3 undefended. Black can immediately exploit this.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn move, look for ways to exploit the undefended pieces or weakened squares. Here, Rfc8 attacks the knight and threatens tactics.
notes.plans: Black plays Rfc8, and after White's Rb3, Black can play Nb8 to reroute the knight to b6 and eventually c4, exploiting the weak c4 square.

notes.explains: Nb8 is a retreating knight maneuver inspired by Nimzowitsch's famous Nh1. The knight will go to b6 and then c4, occupying the weak square.
notes.teaches: Retreating knight moves can be powerful when part of a longer maneuver to reach an outpost. Don't be afraid to move a piece backward if it improves its future prospects.
notes.plans: Black's knight goes to b6 and then c4, while the other knight stays on f6 to pressure e4. White's position is cramped and passive.

notes.explains: Black exchanges on f3, ruining White's kingside pawn structure. Although Black's kingside looks ugly, it is solid and White has no attacking pieces.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically reject a move that weakens your pawn structure if it is unexploitable. Here, the doubled f-pawns are not a target because White lacks the pieces to attack.
notes.plans: Black will play g6 to further solidify the kingside, then continue the knight maneuver to c4. White's only counterplay would be a4, but it's too late.

notes.explains: Nh5 is a surprising move that places the knight on the rim, but it controls key squares g3 and f4, restricting White's knight on e2.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim can be effective if they control critical squares. Here, Nh5 prevents White from generating kingside play and opens a path for the queen to join the attack.
notes.plans: Black's queen will go to d8 and then h4, targeting the weakened kingside. The knight on h5 is annoying for White and can later be redeployed.

notes.explains: Black's Qd8 prepares Qh4, threatening mate on h3. The knight on h5 and the open g-file give Black a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's kingside is weakened, transfer your queen to the attack. The queen on d8 is well-placed to go to h4, exploiting the dark-square weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will play Qh4, forcing White to defend. The tactical blow Nxf4 is possible, but Qh4 is simpler and more effective.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a knight on f4 to open lines against the king. After Bxf4, Qxh3 is mate, so White must play Kh2, but Black's attack continues.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be alert to tactical sacrifices that open lines. Here, Nxf4 is a standard sacrifice to expose the king, even if it's not the only winning move.
notes.plans: After Kh2, Black plays Qxh3+ and then e5 to open the center and bring the knight into the attack. The rook on c6 can lift to f6 or double on the c-file.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, opening the center to bring the knight on b8 into the attack via d7 and e5. This is more effective than a direct knight move.
notes.teaches: When attacking, open the center to involve your pieces. The pawn break e5 gives Black's knight access to e5 and opens the e-file for the rook.
notes.plans: Black plays dxe5, then Nxe5, and the knight on e5 is powerful. The rook on c8 can go to e8 or lift to f6, targeting f2.

notes.explains: Black's Rc6 is a flexible move that keeps the rook on the c-file while preparing to lift it to f6 or double on the c-file. It also eyes the c2 pawn.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, keep your pieces flexible. The rook on c6 can go to f6 to target f2, or stay on the c-file to pressure c2. This adaptability is key.
notes.plans: Black will play Rf6 or double rooks on the c-file, depending on White's response. The immediate threat is Rxf3, winning the pawn on f3.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn with Qxd5, and then Rc8-d8 traps the queen. White's queen has no good squares and must retreat to g2, after which Black picks off the c2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, look for tactics that win material. Here, the queen on d5 is safe because of the threat of Rc8-d8, and White's queen is overloaded.
notes.plans: Black plays Rd8, forcing the queen back, then takes on c2. The game is technically winning, but Black should avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: Black wins the c2 pawn and is up two pawns. The game is technically winning, but Black must be careful not to allow counterplay.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify if possible, but avoid moves that give the opponent counterplay. Here, the simplest win is to take on c2 and consolidate.
notes.plans: Black will trade rooks if possible and use the extra pawns to win. The king should be kept safe, and Black should avoid pawn weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black plays Rxf2, a queen sacrifice that forces checkmate or wins more material. White must take the rook, after which Black's queen delivers mate.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning position, look for the most forcing and beautiful finish. Here, the queen sacrifice is decisive and avoids any technical difficulties.
notes.plans: After Kxf2, Black plays Qf3+ and Qg3#. If White doesn't take, Black is simply up a rook.

notes.explains: The Classical Variation (Be2) is a calm developmental approach favored by Karpov. It avoids tactical complications and aims to convert superior central control into a tangible advantage. Both sides castle kingside, so the battle revolves around central control rather than opposite-side attacks.
notes.teaches: Don't confuse calm development with lack of ambition. The Classical Variation is a dangerous weapon that gives White a lasting edge without needing to memorize sharp lines.

notes.explains: After e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O, Black's main ideas are ...c5, ...e5, or ...c6. Against ...c5, White can play d5 (Benoni-style) or dxc5. Both are playable, but d5 is principled, keeping a central pawn majority.
notes.teaches: In closed center positions, White's key maneuver is Nf3-d2-c4, targeting the weak d6 pawn. This is a standard idea from the Benoni structure.
notes.plans: Play d5 to close the center, then maneuver the knight to c4. Prevent Black's expansion with ...b5 by playing a4 if Black plays ...a6.

notes.explains: Black played ...Qb6, attacking b2. White played Nd2, seemingly blundering the b2 pawn, but after ...Qxb2, Nb5 creates a double threat (Nc7+ and Nxd6) and the queen is in trouble. The knight on d2 also defends e4, a crucial point.
notes.teaches: When your opponent grabs a pawn on b2 with the queen, don't panic. Look for counterplay that exploits the queen's exposed position. A knight on b5 can be devastating.
notes.plans: After Nb5, Black's queen is trapped. The immediate threat is Nc7+, winning the rook. Black's best is ...Nbd7, but White is winning.

notes.explains: To trap the queen on b2, first identify its escape routes (b4, a5, d8). Cover b4 with a3, then play Rb1, forcing the queen to a2. Finally, Bc4 traps it. This requires precise coordination of multiple pieces.
notes.teaches: Trapping a queen is a complex process that often requires many pieces. Don't assume it's easy; look for escape squares and ensure you have enough material to keep the queen trapped without giving up too much in return.
notes.plans: Play a3, then Rb1, then Bc4. Black's best defense is ...Bg4, but f3 repels it. The queen is lost.

notes.explains: After trapping the queen, Black played ...Bh5, which also becomes trapped. White can win it with g4. This shows the importance of making mental notes: while focusing on the queen, don't overlook other hanging pieces.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for additional weaknesses. When your opponent is in trouble, look for secondary targets. A quick mental note can lead to winning more material.
notes.plans: Play g4, winning the bishop. Then simplify and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Up a queen for a rook, White can play Nxd6, deflecting the rook from d6. If ...Rxd6, Qxb7 forks the knight on a6 and the rook on b8. Black can try ...Rb8, but Qxa7 keeps the pressure, and White wins the knight back.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, look for tactics that simplify or win more material. Deflection and forks are common themes. Always calculate until you are sure the tactic works.
notes.plans: Play Nxd6, then Qxb7, winning the exchange and more pawns. Alternatively, play Nc4 for a more symbolic finish.

notes.explains: With a huge material advantage, White's simplest plan is to trade pieces and promote the d-pawn. Alternatively, look for checkmate. Here, Nd6 threatens Qxg6+ and Bf5#. The knight on d6 blocks the king's escape to h5.
notes.teaches: When up massive material, first look for checkmate. If none exists, simplify by trading pieces and pushing passed pawns. Don't get fancy; clinical play is fastest.
notes.plans: Play Nd6, threatening Qxg6+ and Bf5#. If Black defends, simplify and promote the d-pawn.

notes.explains: The choice of Be2 over Bc4 or Bd3 is tactical. Bc4 allows ...Nxe4!? with a fork trick, while Bd3 invites ...Bg4, pressuring d4. Be2 avoids these issues and is more solid.
notes.teaches: In the Pirc, Be2 is the safest and most principled square for the bishop. It avoids tactical tricks and prepares a solid kingside setup.

notes.explains: A common trap: if White plays Bd3 and Black plays ...Bg4, White may try h3, but after ...Bxf3, Qxf3, Nc6, and ...Nd7, White's d4 pawn comes under pressure. A known trick is ...Ne5! hitting the loose bishop on d3, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: Be aware of loose pieces. If your bishop is undefended, your opponent may exploit it with a knight fork or other tactic. Always check for such opportunities.

notes.explains: After Be2, O-O, O-O, a critical tabiya arises. Black's main moves are ...c6, ...e5, and ...c5. Against ...c6, White should play a4 to prevent ...b5 expansion. This is a standard prophylactic idea.
notes.teaches: In the Pirc, if Black plays ...c6, immediately play a4 to stop ...b5. Allowing ...b5 gives Black counterplay and weakens White's center.
notes.plans: After a4, Black often plays ...Nbd7. White can then play h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and later aim for Bc4, trading queens and leaving Black with development problems.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...e5, White can capture twice, leading to an endgame where Black wins back the pawn with ...Nxc4. However, White can avoid this by playing Bg5, pinning the knight and maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: In the ...e5 line, don't automatically recapture. Bg5 is a strong move that prevents Black from equalizing easily. If Black grabs the b2 pawn, White gets a huge attack.
notes.plans: After ...e5, play Bg5. If ...Qxb2, play c3, cutting off the bishop's retreat, and White's attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: In the Benoni-like structure after d5, the knight maneuver Nf3-d2-c4 is essential. It targets the d6 pawn and puts pressure on Black's position. If Black plays ...a6, White should respond with a4 to prevent ...b5.
notes.teaches: The knight on c4 is a monster in these structures. It attacks d6 and supports central expansion. Always look for this maneuver when you have a pawn on d5 and Black has a pawn on d6.
notes.plans: Play Nd2, then Nc4. If Black plays ...a6, play a4. Then continue with moves like f3, Bg4, or other improvements.

notes.explains: A cautionary tale: in a similar position, the player tried to trap the queen but overlooked that Black could sacrifice the queen for three pieces and a dangerous passed pawn. The resulting material imbalance (queen vs. rook and two minor pieces) was insufficient because Black's pieces were active.
notes.teaches: When trapping a queen, ensure you don't give up too many pieces for it. A queen is worth about 9 points, but three minor pieces (9 points) with coordination can be better. Always evaluate the resulting material balance and activity.

notes.explains: In the game, after trapping the queen, White also won the bishop on h5 with g4. This is a classic example of picking low-hanging fruit: when your opponent is in trouble, look for additional hanging pieces before executing more complex tactics.
notes.teaches: Always scan for undefended pieces. Winning a free piece is often better than a flashy tactic. Simplify when possible.

notes.explains: The final mating idea: Qxg6+ and Bf5# requires the knight on d6 to block the king's escape to h5. This pattern (queen sacrifice on g6 followed by bishop to f5) is a common checkmate motif when the king is trapped by its own pawns.
notes.teaches: Recognize mating patterns where a queen sacrifice opens lines. The knight's role in covering escape squares is crucial. Always consider such patterns when the king is boxed in.

notes.explains: White plays d4, opening the center. Black should capture with …cxd4 to avoid an unfavorable queen trade after Qxd4, which would expose the king.
notes.teaches: In Sicilian structures, avoid trading queens early when your king is still in the center, as it often leaves you vulnerable to a lasting initiative.
notes.plans: After …cxd4 Qxd4, Black will develop with ...Nf6, ...e6, and ...Be7, accepting a slight weakness on d5 but aiming to catch up in development.

notes.explains: Black is seriously behind in development. The immediate …Nf6 runs into e5, leading to a poor endgame. Black must first prevent e5 by playing …e5, a typical positional concession to block the center.
notes.teaches: When behind in development, avoid opening the center. A pawn move like ...e5 can be a necessary evil to buy time for development, even if it creates a weakness on d5.
notes.plans: After …e5 Qd3, Black will play ...Be7, ...Nf6, and ...0-0, accepting the d5 weakness as a long-term problem but prioritizing king safety.

notes.explains: Black needs to develop but must avoid the 'Smyslov idea': if Black plays …Nf6 immediately, White can play Bg5, exchanging the knight and then occupying the d5 outpost with a knight. This is a classic strategic pattern.
notes.teaches: When a key outpost (like d5) is contested, be wary of allowing your defender to be exchanged. The Smyslov idea is to remove the defender and then occupy the square.
notes.plans: Black should first play …Be7 to prevent Bg5, then follow with ...Nf6 and ...0-0. If White plays Bg5 anyway, Black can respond with ...h6 to break the pin.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5 anyway. Black must avoid the exchange by playing …h6, forcing the bishop to retreat. This prevents the Smyslov idea and keeps the knight on f6 to contest d5.
notes.teaches: When facing a pin that threatens to exchange your defender, a pawn move like ...h6 can be a useful prophylactic, especially if the bishop has no good retreat that maintains the pin.
notes.plans: After …h6 Bh4, Black will play ...Nf6, ...0-0, and then aim to activate the light-squared bishop and challenge White's center.

notes.explains: Black finally develops the knight to f6. White now has a strong move: Qb4, threatening Qxb7 and also preparing Bb6 to attack the d6 pawn. This puts Black under severe pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a lead in development, they can often create threats that force concessions. Here, Black must deal with the queen's entry on b4.
notes.plans: Black should play …Qd7, defending b7 and preparing to contest the b4 square. Alternatively, …Qe7 is possible but more awkward. The key is to avoid allowing Bb6.

notes.explains: Black played …Qd7, but White has the crushing reply Rd1, threatening Nxe5. If Black plays …Qc6, then Nxe5 dxe5 Rd8# is mate. Black must move the queen again.
notes.teaches: When your queen is attacked and the opponent has a rook on an open file, be alert to back-rank mate threats. Sometimes you must retreat the queen to an awkward square to survive.
notes.plans: Black's only move is …Qe6, blocking the e5 pawn but allowing ...0-0 next. White then plays Bc7, attacking the queen and forcing further concessions.

notes.explains: White plays Bc7, attacking the queen and threatening Nxe5. Black must play …d5 to avoid losing the d6 pawn, but this opens the center and White's attack becomes overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When you are behind in development, a pawn break like ...d5 can be forced, but it often leads to a losing position if the opponent's pieces are better coordinated.
notes.plans: Black plays …d5, hoping to complicate. White can simply capture Nxd5, and after …Nxd5 Qxd5, Black cannot recapture because of mate on d8. Black is lost.

notes.explains: After Qxd5, Black cannot recapture because of mate. The only move is …Qa5, but White has d4, and Black's position collapses. The opening phase is a complete disaster for Black due to the development deficit.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, a single misstep can lead to a decisive disadvantage. It is crucial to know the specific tactical nuances of your repertoire to avoid such catastrophes.
notes.plans: Black will try to survive by giving up material and hoping for counterplay, but White's attack is overwhelming. The game is effectively lost.

notes.explains: The Fantasy Variation (f3) is recommended because it is less studied than main lines and leads to sharp tactical positions where black cannot improvise.
notes.teaches: Choose openings that are less theoretical and force opponents to think early.
notes.plans: After …dxe4 fxe4 e5, white should develop with Nf3, meeting ...Bg4 with Bc4 or c3.

notes.explains: Bc4 is more ambitious than c3; it forces black to know precise theory to avoid traps.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, prioritize active piece development over solidifying the center.
notes.plans: After …Nd7 O-O Ngf6 c3, white solidifies the center and prepares to attack on the f-file.

notes.explains: Black's setup with ...Qe7 prepares queenside castling and threatens ...h5-h4, leading to opposite-side attacks.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent is preparing opposite-side castling and plan your own attack accordingly.
notes.plans: White should complete development with Nbd2, then consider Qa4 or Qb3 to pressure the queenside.

notes.explains: Qa4 provokes ...Kb8, after which the queen drops back to b3 with an x-ray on the b-pawn. This is a practical way to create problems for a well-prepared opponent.
notes.teaches: Use provocative moves to force the opponent out of preparation; even if not objectively best, they create practical difficulties.
notes.plans: After …Kb8 Qb3, white threatens Ba6 and Nc4, pressuring the queenside and the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's ...Nh5 aims to eliminate the dark-squared bishop to relieve pressure on e5. White should not panic with Bxf7; instead, stick to the queenside plan.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a threat, evaluate if it can be ignored or met with a stronger counter-threat.
notes.plans: White should play Ba6, threatening to force ...b6 and then jump the knight to c4, creating serious pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: After …Nb6, white must calculate concretely. The bishop on a6 is hanging, so white needs a tempo-gaining move. Nxe5 is strong because if black recaptures, Nc6 forks the king and queen.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, look for forcing moves that exploit the opponent's loss of control over key squares.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, threatening Nc6+; if black avoids the fork, white wins a pawn and maintains the attack.

notes.explains: Black's ...Be6 is a strong defensive move that white underestimated. It pins the knight and threatens to win material. White must now cut losses and find the best way to give up a piece for maximum compensation.
notes.teaches: When you have miscalculated, accept the loss and look for the most graceful way to minimize damage—often by sacrificing a piece for pawns and long-term pressure.
notes.plans: Play Nxc6+ to force bxc6, then Bxd6+; white gets two pawns and continued pressure against the black king.

notes.explains: White has two pawns for the piece and practical attacking chances. The queen retreats to c2, a flexible square that keeps rooks coordinated and avoids immediate threats.
notes.teaches: When down material, give your opponent as many decisions as possible; open-ended moves can be more effective than forcing lines.
notes.plans: Start pushing the a-pawn (a4-a5) to drive away the knight on b6 and open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: White plays b4 to gain space on the queenside and prevent ...c5. This also gives black more rope to make mistakes.
notes.teaches: When attacking, use pawns to restrict the opponent's options and create targets.
notes.plans: Follow up with a5 to chase the knight away, then consider Bxc8 or Nc4 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Nc4 brings the knight into the attack and threatens tactical ideas. Black must decide where to place the queen.
notes.teaches: Every move should pose a new problem for the opponent, especially when they are short on time.
notes.plans: After black's queen move, play Bxc8 to eliminate the bishop and continue the queenside assault.

notes.explains: White plays g3 to kick the knight from f4 and then capture the f7 pawn. This weakens the king slightly but with reduced material, it's not a problem.
notes.teaches: When down material, look for ways to win back pawns; a minor piece is only three points.
notes.plans: After ...Nh5, play Rxf7, winning a pawn and creating a passed e-pawn. Then use the rook on the seventh rank to generate tactical threats.

notes.explains: After Rxf7, white threatens Nb6+ forking king and queen. The combination of the rook on the seventh rank and the x-ray on the a-file creates a winning tactic.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical motifs like forks, discovered checks, and x-rays when you have a rook on the seventh rank.
notes.plans: Play Nb6+; if ...Nxb6, axb6 wins the queen. If ...Kb8, then Rxf8+ and axb6 is winning.

notes.explains: White's attack culminates in Qa4, threatening mate on a7. Black's king is exposed and white's pieces coordinate perfectly.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, use your queen and rook together to create mating threats; don't be afraid to sacrifice material for a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After ...Kb8, play Qa6 followed by Qb7#. If black tries to block, simply capture the blocking piece.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoed against the Grand Prix Attack, then played d6 and e6 to solidify the center. White's d4 break opened the position; Black responded with cxd4 and developed the knight to e7, a typical Botvinnik-style setup. The bishop on c4 was later retreated to b3 to prevent d5 breaks.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, Black's setup with ...d6 and ...e6 is solid, but combining ...g6 and ...e6 can weaken d6 if White can occupy it. Here, Black controls d6, so the combination is safe.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development with ...b6 and ...Bb7, then challenge White's center with ...d5 or ...e5 breaks.

notes.explains: After White's knight sacrifice on d6, Black played ...f4 to block the kingside and buy time to coordinate pieces. This move hits the bishop on e3 and creates a defensive barrier, making it harder for White to infiltrate.
notes.teaches: When under attack, a pawn advance like ...f4 can serve both offensive (hitting a piece) and defensive (blocking lines) purposes, gaining a tempo to reorganize.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...Qc7 and ...Rfd8 to target the knight on d6, then eventually bring the knight to g6 to solidify the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black is up a piece but must be careful due to White's active rook and potential mating threats. After ...b4, Black missed a drawing resource: White could play Bxa8, leading to a line where ...bxc3, Bf1, c2, Ke2, Na3, Kd1, Nc4, a4! forces a draw by repetition because the knight cannot escape via b5.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a material advantage, prophylaxis is key. Look for ways to neutralize opponent's counterplay before executing your own plan. Here, ...Rc4 would have been safer than ...Rxe4, avoiding complications.
notes.plans: Black should consolidate by bringing the bishop back to g7 and doubling rooks, then slowly convert the extra piece.

notes.explains: Black missed the winning continuation after ...b4. Instead of Bxa8, White played Rxf7, allowing Black to win with Nf3+! The knight fork wins the game because after gxf3, Rxe7, Rxa8, Bxc3, Black is up a full rook.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical resources like knight forks, especially when the opponent's king is exposed. A fresh perspective can reveal winning moves that are easy to overlook.
notes.plans: After Nf3+, Black wins material and should convert by activating the remaining pieces.

notes.explains: After white castles queenside, the king and queen are aligned on the same diagonal. This makes Bh6 a powerful pin, threatening the queen.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, look for pins along the diagonal from h6 to d2. Bh6 can be a devastating resource when white's queen is on d2.
notes.plans: Play Ng4, threatening Bh6. If white plays f4, then e5 attacks the pawn and the bishop on d4, winning a piece.

notes.explains: Black plays Bh6 pinning the queen. White's best is to retreat the bishop to e3, but then black captures on e3, ruining white's pawn structure. If white plays f4, black has e5, attacking f4 and the bishop on d4.
notes.teaches: When a bishop pins the queen, a pawn break like e5 can exploit the pin by attacking the pinned piece and another target simultaneously.
notes.plans: After Bh6, if white plays f4, play e5. If white retreats to e3, capture with the knight and enjoy the damaged pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, attacking f4 and the bishop on d4. White loses at least a piece because the pawn on f4 is pinned and cannot capture.
notes.teaches: A pinned pawn cannot defend. Attack it with another pawn to create a double attack.
notes.plans: After e5, white's best is Bxe5 Nxe5, leaving black up a piece. Continue developing and attacking.

notes.explains: Black is up a piece but must be careful. The tempting Bxf4+ is a mistake because after Kb1, black's bishop on f4 hangs. Instead, take on d4 immediately.
notes.teaches: When winning, avoid greedy pawn grabs that expose your pieces. Calculate carefully before taking a pawn with check.
notes.plans: Take on d4 with the knight. If Qxd4, then Nxc3. If white recaptures, then Bxf4+ is safe.

notes.explains: Black is up a piece and white's queenside is shattered. The pawn on c3 can be used as a battering ram to open lines against the white king.
notes.teaches: When attacking a castled king, use pawns to break open the pawn shield. A pawn on c3 can force b3 or cxb3, creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play Qb6 threatening Qa3#. If white plays b3, then Qa3 is mate. If white plays cxb3, then Qf6 or Qa5 attacks the c3 pawn and the king.

notes.explains: Qb6 threatens Qa3#. White can defend with Rd2, but then black can play d5 to open the center and bring the bishop to f5, or play Bg4 to force Rd8 and then Qa3.
notes.teaches: When the king is stuck on c1, the threat of Qa3# is powerful. Use the rook on d8 to cover the d1 escape square, and open the center to prevent the king from running.
notes.plans: Play d5 to open the center, or Bg4 to force Rd8, then Qa3#. If white plays Ka1, then Qa3 is still mate after Rook moves.

notes.explains: Black opens the center with d5, activating the light-squared bishop and preventing the white king from escaping via d1.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, open lines to expose it. A central pawn break can be decisive.
notes.plans: After d5, if exd5, then Bf5 attacking the rook on d2. If white doesn't capture, then dxe4 opens the d-file.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the rook on d2 and threatens to capture. White cannot take because of Qxd2. This forces white to move the king or block, allowing black to play Rd8 and then Qa3#.
notes.teaches: Use pins to immobilize defenders and create threats. Bg4 here forces a winning attack.
notes.plans: After Bg4, if white plays Kb1, then Rd8 and Qa3#. If white plays f3, then Bxf3 wins the exchange.

notes.explains: Rd8 covers d1, making Qa3 an unstoppable mate threat. White cannot prevent Qa3#.
notes.teaches: After covering the king's escape square, a queen check on a3 can be mate. This is the 'lobster pincer mate' pattern.
notes.plans: Play Qa3#. If white blocks with Bd3, then Rxd3 cxd3 Qxd3+ Kb1 Qd2#.

notes.explains: The key difference between the Accelerated Dragon and the mainline Dragon is that black saves a tempo on d6. This allows black to play d5 in one go if white plays f3.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, avoid playing d6 early. Keep the pawn on d7 to meet f3 with d5, which is often very strong.
notes.plans: If white plays f3, play d5 immediately. After Nxd5 Nxd5 exd5, black has active pieces and white's structure is damaged.

notes.explains: If white tries to punish black's lack of d6 by playing Nxc6 and e5, black can retreat the knight to g8 and redeploy via h6 to f5. This is a known maneuver.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to move a piece backward if it leads to a good square. The knight can go from f6 to g8 to h6 to f5, and this cannot be punished easily.
notes.plans: After e5, play Ng8, then Nh6, then Nf5. Black's structure is solid and the knight becomes active.

notes.explains: In the position after Nxc6 bxc6 Bd4, black should not trade bishops on d4. Instead, play e5 to close the diagonal, even though it temporarily blocks the bishop. Trading the dark-squared bishop is a concession.
notes.teaches: In Dragon setups, do not give up your fianchettoed bishop for white's bishop unless forced. It is better to play e5 and keep the bishop, even if it is temporarily blocked.
notes.plans: Play e5, then develop and prepare d6 or other breaks. The bishop can be reactivated later.

notes.explains: The Bh6 idea is a recurring tactic in many Sicilian lines, especially when white's queen is on d2 and the king has castled queenside. Players often miss this because it seems unnatural to move the bishop from its fianchetto.
notes.teaches: Always look for Bh6 in Dragon and similar Sicilian positions. It can pin the queen and lead to devastating attacks.

notes.explains: Black chooses a Grünfeld-like setup with g6, but White's pawn is on e4 rather than c4, leading to a fundamentally different game.
notes.teaches: The Jobava London often arises after d4 Nc3, and if Black plays d5, White can push e4 to reach this sharp, tactical line.
notes.plans: White aims to launch a kingside attack with h4-h5, often sacrificing the exchange on h5 to open lines.

notes.explains: White immediately pushes the h-pawn, a key idea in this line. If Black allows h5, White can sacrifice the exchange on h5 for a powerful attack.
notes.teaches: Early h-pawn pushes can be legitimate, especially when Black has fianchettoed. The idea is to open the h-file and create attacking chances.
notes.plans: White wants to play h5, and if Black takes, recapture with the rook, then follow up with Qh5, threatening d5 and other weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black stops h5 with h5, freezing the kingside structure. White continues development with Nf3, preparing to castle queenside and later play g4.
notes.teaches: When the h-pawn is blocked, White can still prepare g4 to break open the kingside. The attack often involves opposite-side castling.
notes.plans: White castles queenside, then plays g4 to force open the h-file, using the queen and rooks to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, a typical queenside counter. White cannot play c3 to support d4, but the knight on c3 eyes d5. White can capture on c5 or play Ne5.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, c5 is a common response. White must decide whether to take on c5 or maintain the pawn on d4. The knight on c3 provides pressure on d5.
notes.plans: White can consider dxc5, but the recommended move is Ne5, preparing f3 and g4. Taking on c5 can lead to complications if Black knows the theory.

notes.explains: White played dxc5, but this is a mistake. Black responds with Nbd7, threatening to recapture on c5 and also eyeing d5. White cannot take on d5 due to tactics.
notes.teaches: Taking on c5 can be dangerous if Black knows the refutation. The move Nbd7 is strong because it prepares to recapture and keeps d5 defended indirectly.
notes.plans: White must now play Ne5 to avoid losing material. The position is tricky, and White should have played Ne5 earlier instead of dxc5.

notes.explains: White plays Ne5 and f3, preparing g4 and controlling e4. The knight on e5 is well-placed, and f3 prevents Black's knights from jumping to e4.
notes.teaches: f3 serves two purposes: it prepares the g4 break and restricts Black's knights. Controlling e4 is crucial to maintain the attack.
notes.plans: White will castle queenside and then play g4 to open the kingside. The queen on d2 can later move to h2 to threaten checkmate.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to f5, eyeing the queenside. White considers g4 but decides it's premature. Instead, White castles queenside to safety.
notes.teaches: When opposite-side castling, it's important to secure your king before launching the attack. g4 can be delayed if it's not fully prepared.
notes.plans: White castles queenside (O-O-O), then prepares g4. The immediate threat is Nxd5, but White must be careful about tactics on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black retreats the bishop to e6, a passive move that loses time. This gives White the opportunity to play g4 now that the king is safe.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, every tempo counts. Black's passive move allows White to seize the initiative with the g4 break.
notes.plans: White plays g4 to open the kingside. The queen on d2 can go to h2, threatening checkmate on h7. Black's bishop on e6 is misplaced.

notes.explains: White plays g4, the thematic break. Black can take on g4, but White then recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file and preparing h5.
notes.teaches: The g4 break is a classic attacking idea in fianchetto positions. It opens lines for the rooks and queen, often leading to a devastating attack.
notes.plans: If Black takes on g4, White recaptures with f3xg4, then pushes h5. The queen can go to h2, and the rooks join the attack via the h-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa5, pressuring a2 and the queenside. White responds with Kb1, a standard defensive move that also sets up a tactical threat.
notes.teaches: When opposite-side castling, it's crucial to defend your king. Kb1 is a typical move that also prepares potential tactics like Nxd5.
notes.plans: White threatens Nxd5, which would win material due to the discovered attack on the queen. Black must be careful not to fall for this tactic.

notes.explains: Black plays Rfc8, bringing the rook to the c-file. White now has the tactical opportunity Nxd5, which wins material due to the queen on a5.
notes.teaches: When the queen is on a5 and the rook on c8, Nxd5 can be a powerful tactic. Black cannot recapture because the queen would be lost.
notes.plans: White plays Nxd5. If Black captures the queen, White recaptures with the rook and then plays Nxe7+, winning a pawn. The knight may be trapped, but White can try to extricate it.

notes.explains: White executes the tactic: Nxd5, forcing queen trade, then Nxe7+ winning a pawn. Black's king moves to h8, and White recaptures on d5, emerging with two extra pawns.
notes.teaches: This sequence illustrates a classic desperado tactic: when a piece is attacked, you can often sacrifice it for material gain if you have intermediate checks.
notes.plans: White is up two pawns but the knight on e7 is trapped. White must find a way to save the knight, possibly by playing g5 to open lines or by sacrificing it for more pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays Rxc2, attacking the bishop on f4 and threatening back-rank mate. White must respond carefully to avoid losing the knight on e7.
notes.teaches: After a sequence of exchanges, it's easy to overlook threats like back-rank mate. Always update your perception of the board after each exchange.
notes.plans: White can play Rd4, a collinear move that defends the rook and prepares to extricate the knight. Alternatively, White can play Nxg6, sacrificing the knight for pawns.

notes.explains: White plays Rd4, a collinear move that places the rook on a defended square (by the pawn on e4) while keeping the file open. This defends against back-rank threats and prepares to save the knight.
notes.teaches: A collinear move is when you move a piece onto the same line as two opposing pieces, but not capturing. It can be a powerful defensive or tactical idea.
notes.plans: White threatens Nxg6, winning more pawns. Black must respond, and White can then extricate the knight via d5 or g8.

notes.explains: Black captures on g4. White now has the opportunity to play h5, opening the h-file and threatening the knight on h5. The knight on e7 is also well-placed to support the attack.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, even after queens are traded, the h-file can still be a decisive attacking avenue. The knight on e7 can aid in checkmate patterns.
notes.plans: White plays h5, threatening to open the h-file. If Black captures on h5, White recaptures with the pawn, opening lines. The knight on e7 prevents the black king from escaping.

notes.explains: Black captures on h5. White now plays fxg4, opening the f-file and threatening the knight on h5. The knight on e7 is pinned, and White can win material.
notes.teaches: When the h-file is opened, the rook on h1 becomes a powerful attacker. The pinned knight on h5 is vulnerable, and White can exploit it.
notes.plans: White plays fxg4, threatening to capture the knight on h5. Black's best try is to play Bxg4, but then White has Rxd8+ and other tactics.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxg4, trying to gain material. White can now play Rxd8+ and then Nxg6+, winning the rook on f8 and the bishop on g4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to counterattack, look for intermediate checks and captures that win material. Avoid tunnel vision and consider all tactical possibilities.
notes.plans: White plays Rxd8+ first, then Nxg6+ forking king and rook. After the king moves, White captures the rook on f8, winning a huge amount of material.

notes.explains: White executes the winning sequence: Rxd8+, Nxg6+, and Nxf8, emerging with a rook and multiple pawns for two pieces. The knight on e7 is safe and can be evacuated.
notes.teaches: This sequence demonstrates how to convert a material advantage by forcing exchanges and simplifying. The knight on e7 can later be brought to d5 or f4.
notes.plans: White is up a rook and several pawns. The knight on e7 can be evacuated via d5 or g8. White should consolidate and then push for checkmate or further material gain.

notes.explains: White plays Nd5, evacuating the knight to a safe square. The knight is well-placed in the center, and White can now bring the bishop into play.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, centralize your pieces. The knight on d5 is strong and can later move to f4 or e3 to support the attack.
notes.plans: White will bring the bishop to d3 or e2, then use the rook to target Black's weak pawns. The knight can go to f4 to pressure h5.

notes.explains: White plays Nf4, targeting the pawn on h5 and creating a strong outpost. The knight is defended by the pawn on g2 and cannot be easily dislodged.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, knights on outposts can be very powerful. Nf4 attacks h5 and supports a future advance of the kingside pawns.
notes.plans: White will play Bg2 or Bd3, then push the kingside pawns. Black's pawn on h5 is weak and can be captured.

notes.explains: Black plays Rc5, attacking the pawn on g5. White can defend with Bg2 or simply advance the pawn. The position is winning for White.
notes.teaches: When up material, it's often best to simplify. White can trade rooks or bishops to reduce Black's counterplay.
notes.plans: White can play Bg2, then Rg3 or Rh3. Alternatively, White can play g6 to open lines. The key is to avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, activating the bishop and threatening to trade on f5. This simplifies the position and removes Black's active bishop.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. Bd3 forces Black to either trade or retreat, both of which favor White.
notes.plans: After Bd3, White can play Rg3 or Rh3. The knight on f4 is well-placed, and White can push the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: White pushes g6, opening lines and threatening to create a passed pawn. Black's rook is passive, and White's knight and rook are active.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, creating passed pawns is a key winning method. g6 opens the f-file and supports the advance of the h-pawn.
notes.plans: White will play Rh3 or Rg3, then push the h-pawn. Black's king is cut off, and White's pieces dominate.

notes.explains: White plays Nd5, forking the rook and pawn on e7. Black must give up material. The knight is a powerful piece in this endgame.
notes.teaches: Knights are often stronger than rooks in closed positions. Nd5 creates a double threat that wins material.
notes.plans: After Nd5, Black will lose the pawn on e7 or the rook. White will then have a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6 to decline the Morra Gambit and transpose into an Alapin Sicilian, avoiding the sharp tactical lines of the accepted Morra.
notes.teaches: Against the Smith-Morra, declining with Nf6 is a safe and reputable way to steer the game into Alapin territory, where Black's knowledge can neutralize White's initiative.
notes.plans: Black aims to solidify the center and develop naturally, targeting White's d4-pawn.

notes.explains: After the main line with Bc4, Black can deviate with d6 and Be6, followed by g6 and Bg7. This setup blocks the bishop's diagonal but allows fianchetto development, challenging White's center.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, Black can use the ...Be6 and ...g6 setup to create a solid but flexible structure, often leading to positions where White's development is awkward.
notes.plans: Black will castle kingside and target White's e5-pawn with ...Bg7 and ...Qb6, pressuring the center.

notes.explains: If White plays Ng5, Black exchanges bishops and blocks the check with Qd7, then develops Bg7. The knight on d5 is well-supported by the e6-pawn, and Black's position is comfortable.
notes.teaches: In these lines, Black should prioritize development and not fear the exchange of light-squared bishops, as the resulting structure favors Black's central control.
notes.plans: Black will castle, then target White's center with moves like ...Qb6 and ...Rac8, exploiting White's lack of coordination.

notes.explains: After castling, Black plays Qc7 to defend the knight and prepare ...Rad8. White's pieces are somewhat passive, and Black has a slight edge.
notes.teaches: In IQP-like positions, Black's plan is to pressure the d5-pawn and exploit White's slightly exposed king.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rad8, ...b6, and ...Bb7, increasing pressure on d5 and the queenside.

notes.explains: Black has fully developed and now threatens ...Nxd5. White's pieces are awkwardly placed, and Black's central control gives a comfortable advantage.
notes.teaches: When White's development lags, Black should complete development and then target the center, often with ...Nxd5 or ...b5 to create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black can play ...b5 to chase the queen, then ...Nxd5, winning a pawn or forcing concessions.

notes.explains: Black launches a kingside pawn storm with ...g5 and ...f5, chasing the knight and opening lines. White's position becomes critical.
notes.teaches: When White's king is exposed, Black should not hesitate to advance pawns to open lines and create direct threats.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...f4, ...g4, and ...h5, aiming to open the kingside and deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: Black's pawns advance relentlessly, and White's knight is forced to retreat. Black's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: A coordinated pawn storm can suffocate the opponent's pieces and create mating threats, especially when the opponent's king is poorly defended.
notes.plans: Black will play ...h4, ...g3, and ...Qf5, with ideas of ...Rf8 and ...Rf6 to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange to open lines, and the queen joins the attack. White's king is exposed, and Black has a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing material to open lines against the enemy king is worth it, especially when the opponent's pieces are undeveloped.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rf8, ...Rf6, and ...Rh6, with ideas of ...Qh5 and ...Rh2 checkmate.

notes.explains: Black's attack culminates in a forced checkmate. White's king is hunted down the board.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, a coordinated attack with queen and rooks can lead to a quick checkmate, even if material is equal.

notes.explains: The game ends in a beautiful checkmate, demonstrating the power of a coordinated attack.
notes.teaches: Even in the endgame, a king hunt can lead to checkmate if the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces are active.

notes.explains: White captures on c5, forcing black's bishop to recapture and lose a tempo. This opens the d-file and increases white's development advantage.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has just developed a piece, capturing a pawn that it must recapture gains a tempo. This is a common idea in many openings.
notes.plans: White will now play Qe2 to prepare Rd1, putting pressure on the d-file and eyeing e4 for the queen.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2, preparing Rd1 and keeping the queen active. The queen on e2 is flexible and can later go to e4 or h5.
notes.teaches: Place the queen in the center where it can support multiple ideas. Avoid putting the queen behind the bishop in a battery; the queen should be in front for maximum effect.
notes.plans: White will play Rd1, then Bg5 to pressure the knight on f6, and look for tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to g5, pinning the knight and increasing pressure. Black's queen on c7 is awkward.
notes.teaches: Pin the knight to increase pressure. If black plays h6, the bishop can retreat to h4 and later g3, maintaining pressure while the queen on c7 has few good squares.
notes.plans: White aims to force a favorable trade or create tactical threats. The knight on c4 can go to e5 if black pushes b5.

notes.explains: Black pushes b5, but the knight goes to e5 as planned. After trades, white has pressure and threats like Bxf6 forcing a recapture with a pawn, opening lines.
notes.teaches: When your knight is attacked, move it to a strong central square. The knight on e5 is powerful and can lead to tactics involving the f6 knight.
notes.plans: White can consider Bxh7+ to win a pawn, leading to an endgame with a slight advantage, or continue pressuring with Bh4 and later Bg3.

notes.explains: White plays Bxh7+, forcing the king to capture, then Qd3 forks the knight on d7. This wins a pawn but gives up the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+) can be used to win a pawn when the king is drawn out and the queen can fork another piece. Always calculate the resulting endgame.
notes.plans: After the sequence, white is up a pawn but black has the bishop pair. White will aim to simplify and convert the pawn in the endgame.

notes.explains: White wins a pawn and enters an endgame up a pawn. Black has the bishop pair but white's position is solid.
notes.teaches: When up a pawn, simplification is generally good, but be careful not to give up too much activity. Here, the trade of bishops is acceptable.
notes.plans: White will consolidate, activate the rooks, and create a passed pawn. The king should be brought to the center in the endgame.

notes.explains: Black avoids the queen trade and plays Qb6, threatening to trap the white queen. White retreats to d2, protecting f2.
notes.teaches: When your queen is in danger, retreat to a safe square that also defends key points. Here, Qd2 protects f2 and keeps the queen active.
notes.plans: White will aim to simplify further, possibly trading queens, and then create a passed pawn on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, attacking the bishop. White retreats to e3, offering a trade of bishops. Simplification is good for white as he is up a pawn.
notes.teaches: When up material, trade pieces to reduce the opponent's counterplay. Even if it creates an isolated pawn, the pawn advantage is more important.
notes.plans: After the trade, white will control the d-file and activate the knight, aiming for an outpost on c5.

notes.explains: White trades bishops, leaving an endgame with queen and knight vs queen and bishop. White is up a pawn and has a solid position.
notes.teaches: In queen and minor piece endgames, the side with the extra pawn should aim to create a passed pawn and trade queens when favorable.
notes.plans: White will activate the knight, aiming for c5, and use the queen to support the passed pawn. The king should be brought to safety.

notes.explains: White plays Ne1, preparing f3 to blunt black's bishop battery on the long diagonal. This frees the knight to go to d3 and later c5.
notes.teaches: When your knight is tied down by an enemy bishop battery, move it away and block the diagonal with a pawn. This is a common defensive and regrouping idea.
notes.plans: After f3, the knight will go to d3 and then to c5, supported by b4. White will double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: White prepares b4 to support the knight on c5. Rc1 is a preparatory move, not committing to anything else.
notes.teaches: Prepare pawn advances with rook moves that are non-committal. Rc1 defends c3 and prepares b4 without weakening the position.
notes.plans: White will play b4, then Nc5, creating a strong outpost. If black doubles rooks on the d-file, white can double rooks as well.

notes.explains: Black doubles rooks on the d-file, preventing b4. White responds by doubling rooks as well, maintaining control.
notes.teaches: When your plan is blocked, adapt. Doubling rooks on the open file is a standard way to increase pressure and prepare piece maneuvers.
notes.plans: White will move the knight away from d3, then trade rooks and aim for a queen and knight endgame with an extra pawn.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, white wins a second pawn and simplifies to a queen and knight vs queen and bishop endgame with two extra pawns.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by keeping pieces safe. Nc3 is a solid square, protecting the pawns and avoiding forks.
notes.plans: White will trade queens if possible, then create a passed pawn and promote it. The king should be brought to the center.

notes.explains: White trades queens, entering a rook and knight vs rook and bishop endgame with two extra pawns. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, trading queens simplifies the position and reduces counterplay. Always be ready to trade if it favors you.
notes.plans: White will bring the king to the center, create a passed pawn, and push it. The knight can support the pawn and the rook can cut off the enemy king.

notes.explains: White brings the king to f2, centralizing it. The king will go to d4 to support the pawns and restrict the black king.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king should be active. Centralize the king to support pawn advances and limit the opponent's king activity.
notes.plans: White will play c4, creating a passed pawn on the queenside. The knight can defend while the rook supports the pawn.

notes.explains: White sacrifices two pawns for a big lead in development and central control, aiming for a quick attack.
notes.teaches: In gambits, development and initiative often outweigh material; black must neutralize White's lead before cashing in the extra pawns.
notes.plans: Black should accept the gambit pawns but then carefully coordinate pieces to blunt White's attack and consolidate the material advantage.

notes.explains: White offers the first pawn with c3. Black can accept or decline; declining with d5 is a practical alternative that leads to equal but comfortable positions.
notes.teaches: Declining a gambit with a central counterstrike can take the fun out of White's attack and lead to a solid position.
notes.plans: After …d5, White's best is exd5; black recaptures with the queen, then develops with Nc6 and Bb4+, aiming for an endgame where White's isolated d-pawn is a weakness.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the knight, offering only one pawn. Black must avoid Nf6 due to e5; instead develop the dark-squared bishop to c5 and solidify with d6.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, delaying knight development can prevent tactical shots like e5. Prioritize bishop development and pawn solidity.
notes.plans: Play Bc5, d6, then Nf6 after White's e5 is neutralized. If White plays Qb3, counter with Qh4 attacking f2. After g3, drop back to f6, then e7 to stop Nd5 and prepare Nf6.

notes.explains: White offers a second pawn with Bc4. Black should accept with Nf6, not the old D5 line which gives White easy equality. After e5, check with Bb4.
notes.teaches: Accepting the second pawn is principled; the old D5 sacrifice is outdated. The check on b4 forces White to defend awkwardly.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then after e5, Bb4+. Against most White replies (Nc3, Nd2, Kf1), counter with d5. Against the best reply Bc3, play Qe7 pinning the e-pawn and preparing to redeploy the knight via g8-h6.

notes.explains: White blocks the check with Nc3, the most common move, but it loses on the spot. Black plays d5, counterattacking the center.
notes.teaches: When White's pieces are hanging, a central pawn break can exploit the lack of coordination. Here d5 attacks both the bishop and knight.
notes.plans: After …d5, if exf6, recapture with the queen (Qxf6) hitting both the knight and bishop. White cannot defend both, so Black wins at least a pawn with a winning position.

notes.explains: White moves the king. Black again plays d5, leading to an endgame where White gets a pawn on g7. Black's plan is to surround and win that pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a single extra pawn is often decisive if the opponent has no counterplay. Patience and accurate technique are required.
notes.plans: After exf6, play Qxf6, then develop with Nc6, Bf5, and rook to g8. Target the g7 pawn with moves like Nd7, f6, and Bg6. White's king is exposed, giving Black additional attacking chances.

notes.explains: White blocks with the bishop, the best but rare move. Black should not play d5 here; instead play Qe7, pinning the e-pawn and guarding the bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's best move is rare, it's still essential to know the correct response. Pinning a pawn can prevent a dangerous advance.
notes.plans: Play Qe7. If White takes on b4, recapture with the queen and then play Nd2-e4 with initiative. If White plays Qe2, retreat the knight to g8 and redeploy to h6, then castle and aim for d6 to trade off the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 d5 Bf4, White's Nc3 instead of c3 exerts pressure on d5. Black's c5 is a mistake because dxc5 leaves Black struggling to regain the pawn without falling behind in development. a3 prepares b4 to secure the c5 pawn, and after e5 Bg5, Black must waste a tempo with Be6 to prevent Bxf6 Nxd5. b4 then secures the pawn, leaving White up a pawn with no compensation.
