notes.teaches: When the opponent attacks your centralized bishop, consider moving a knight to e5 to create tactical threats. The knight on e5 often threatens Qa4+ or Bb5+, exploiting the undefended rook on a8.
notes.plans: After Ne5, Black typically plays ...a6 to prevent Bb5+. Then White can consider dxc5 or Bd3. The main idea is to keep pressure and avoid premature exchanges that would relieve Black's cramp.

notes.explains: White plays dxc5, leading to an endgame after ...Nxe3 Qxd8+ Kxd8 fxe3. White is a pawn up but has a doubled e-pawn and Black has the bishop pair. The position is complex; White's extra pawn is balanced by structural weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When deciding to enter an endgame with an extra pawn, consider whether the pawn structure and piece activity compensate. Here, White's pawn on c5 is weak but can be supported by b4, while Black's bishops are passive if White plays correctly.
notes.plans: After fxe3, White should play b4 to secure the c5 pawn and limit Black's dark-squared bishop. Then aim to develop the bishop to e2 or d3, and eventually contest the d-file with the king or rook.

notes.explains: White plays b4 to fix the pawn on c5 and restrict Black's dark-squared bishop. The pawn chain b4-c5 limits Black's bishop to f6 or g7, where it is less effective. White's knight on e5 is well-placed but may need to move if Black plays ...f6.
notes.teaches: In endgames with an extra pawn, creating a pawn chain can restrict the opponent's pieces. Here, b4-c5 keeps Black's dark-squared bishop passive and prevents counterplay on the queenside.
notes.plans: After b4, White should prepare to move the knight to c4 if Black plays ...f6. The knight on c4 eyes b6 and d6, and can be supported by the king or rook. White should also consider playing a4 to prevent ...Bb5 ideas.

notes.explains: White plays Be2, preparing to meet ...Bd7 with Bf3, contesting the long diagonal. This prevents Black's light-squared bishop from becoming active on c6 or b5. The move is prophylactic, stopping Black's main counterplay.
notes.teaches: In endgames, anticipate your opponent's plans. Here, Black wants to develop the light-squared bishop to c6. White preempts this by playing Be2, ready to answer ...Bd7 with Bf3, neutralizing the bishop.
notes.plans: After Be2, if Black plays ...Bd7, White plays Bf3. If Black plays ...Rd8+, White moves the king to c2. The knight on c4 is well-placed; avoid moving it prematurely. Consider a4 to further restrict Black's bishop.

notes.explains: Black develops the dark-squared bishop to g7, threatening ...Bf6 with tempo on the knight. White responds with Nc4, moving the knight to a flexible square. The knight on c4 eyes b6 and d6, and avoids the tempo loss.
notes.teaches: When your knight is attacked with tempo, move it to a square where it remains active and flexible. Nc4 is often better than Nf3 because it keeps pressure on the queenside and can later go to b6 or d6.
notes.plans: After Nc4, White should consider Kd2 to defend c3, or a4 to prevent ...Bb5. The knight should stay on c4 for now; only move it when necessary. Black's bishop on g7 looks impressive but has no targets.

notes.explains: Black plays ...a5, threatening to open the a-file or play ...axb4. White responds with a4, preventing ...Bb5 and keeping the queenside closed. This is a prophylactic move that maintains White's pawn structure and restricts Black's bishop.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis is crucial in endgames. Here, a4 stops Black's bishop from using b5 or a4 squares, and also prevents any ...a5xb4 ideas. Always consider what your opponent wants and try to prevent it.
notes.plans: After a4, White can continue with Bf3 to contest the long diagonal. The knight on c4 is well-placed. White should aim to control the d-file with a rook, and eventually push the kingside pawn majority.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bf6, threatening to exchange bishops or pressure c3. White responds with Bf3, contesting the long diagonal and neutralizing Black's bishop. The bishop on f3 is well-defended and prevents Black from activating the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent places a bishop on a strong diagonal, contest it with your own bishop. Bf3 is a good square because it is defended by a pawn and also eyes b7, potentially creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Bf3, White should consider Rd1 to contest the d-file. The knight on c4 remains flexible. White's plan is to slowly improve the king and pawns, and eventually create a passed pawn on the kingside.

notes.explains: After the exchange of bishops on f3, White plays Rd1 to contest the d-file. Black's rook on c8 is passive. White's knight on c4 is perfectly placed, controlling key squares. The pawn on c5 is secure, and White has a kingside pawn majority.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, controlling the open file is crucial. Here, Rd1 challenges Black's only active piece (the rook) and prepares to double rooks or invade. The knight on c4 is better than a rook on d1 because it controls more squares.
notes.plans: After Rd1, White should aim to double rooks on the d-file or push the kingside pawns. The knight can stay on c4 for now. Black is paralyzed and can only make waiting moves.

notes.explains: White plays Rd6, a classic maneuver to prepare doubling rooks on the d-file. The rook on d6 controls the file and supports a future Rd1. Black's rook on g8 is passive. White's king moves to d2 to defend c3.
notes.teaches: To gain full control of a file, sometimes you need to place a rook on a specific square to prepare doubling. Rd6 is better than Rd4 because it leaves the d4 square open for the king or knight.
notes.plans: After Rd6, White plans to play Rd1, doubling rooks. Then the king can go to c2 or b3. The knight on c4 should stay put. Eventually, White will push the kingside pawns to create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black exchanges rooks on d6, and White recaptures with the knight (not the pawn). The knight on d6 is well-placed, controlling key squares. White then plays Rd1, bringing the other rook to the d-file.
notes.teaches: When recapturing in endgames, consider which piece gives more activity. Here, recapturing with the knight keeps the pawn structure intact and gives the knight a strong outpost on d6. The pawn recapture would create weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Rd1, White has full control of the d-file. The knight on d6 is powerful. White should now improve the king (e.g., Kc2) and prepare to push the kingside pawns. Black is completely passive.

notes.explains: White plays Ne4, moving the knight to a square that prevents Black from playing ...f5 and ...g4 to create a passed pawn. The knight on e4 eyes f6 and g5, freezing Black's kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: In endgames, preventing the opponent's counterplay is often more important than immediate material gain. Here, Ne4 stops Black's plan of ...f5 and ...g4, which would create a passed pawn. Prophylaxis again.
notes.plans: After Ne4, White can push the kingside pawns (e.g., f4, e4, e5) to create a passed pawn. The knight on e4 is well-placed and can later move to f4 or g5. Black's bishop on f6 is passive.

notes.explains: White plays f4, attacking Black's bishop on e5 (after ...Bxe5). This tactical sequence wins a pawn: after ...Bxf4, Nxf6+ Kxf6?? loses to Rxd7, but Black can play ...Kg7. However, White wins the h5 pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for tactical blows that win material. Here, f4 exploits the pin on the d-file and the knight's fork on f6. Calculation is essential to ensure the sequence works.
notes.plans: After f4, if Black captures, White wins a pawn. The resulting position is winning due to White's extra pawn and active pieces. White should then push the passed pawns on the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays c4, fixing the queenside pawns and preparing to create a passed pawn. Black's king is active but White's pawns are mobile. The move c4 also prevents Black's bishop from using c3.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a material advantage, fix the opponent's pawns and create passed pawns. Here, c4 prepares b5 and a6, creating a distant passed pawn that is hard for Black to stop.
notes.plans: After c4, White should play b5 and a6, creating a passed a-pawn. The king can support the pawns. Black's bishop is tied to defending the queenside, and White's knight can help push the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: White plays Nd3, extricating the knight from the bishop's attack. The knight is now free to support the pawns. Black's bishop on c3 is annoying but White's king can move to e4 to dislodge it.
notes.teaches: When your knight is pinned or attacked, look for a safe square where it can still be active. Nd3 is a good square because it defends the b4 pawn and can later go to f4 or e5.
notes.plans: After Nd3, White should play b5 and a6 to create a passed a-pawn. The king can go to e4 to attack the bishop. The knight can also help push the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: White plays c6, creating a passed pawn on the queenside. The pawn on c6 is a distant passer that Black's king and bishop cannot easily stop. White's knight and king can support the pawn.
notes.teaches: Creating a passed pawn on the opposite side of the board from the opponent's king is a winning strategy. Here, c6 forces Black to deal with the a-pawn, while White's king can help push the kingside pawns.
notes.plans: After c6, White should push a6 and a7, queening the a-pawn. Black's bishop is tied to defending the queenside. White's knight can also create threats on the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays c4 to chase the knight. Black retreats to b6, maintaining pressure on c4. White now needs to develop while supporting the center.
notes.teaches: Delay Nf3 until Black's bishop goes to f5; if Black plays Bg4, the pin is annoying. Start with Nc3 and Be3, then develop the kingside after Black commits.
notes.plans: After ...Bf5, play Nf3. Then develop the light-squared bishop to d3, aiming to trade bishops and open the f-file.

notes.explains: After trading bishops and castling, White has a large center and an open f-file. Black's queenside is undeveloped. The key defensive idea for Black is ...c5, but White can meet it with d5, as the d5-square has two defenders (c4-pawn and Nc3) against two attackers.
notes.teaches: When you have a big center, always check that ...c5 can be met with d5. Count defenders and attackers on that square.
notes.plans: White considers aggressive plans: g4 to prepare Ng5, or positional play with Be3. The immediate threat is Ng5, attacking f7.

notes.explains: White plays g4, preparing Ng5 and threatening a kingside attack. The downside is that after ...h6, the knight on c3 moves away, weakening control of d5, so ...c5 becomes possible. But White has a tactical idea: after ...h6, Nfd6!? (or Ncd6) exploits the fork on c5 if Black captures twice.
notes.teaches: When launching an attack, be aware of potential counterplay in the center. Sometimes you can ignore it if your attack is fast enough, but always calculate.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...h6, White can play Nfd6, threatening c5 fork. If Black ignores, Ng5 is devastating.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nc6 instead of ...h6, ignoring the kingside threat. White now has a choice: play Nfg5 immediately, or continue with g5, etc. The key is that after Nfg5, if Black plays ...h6, White has the deflection Nxe6! winning material.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is pushed (like ...h6), other pawns become weaker. Look for tactics exploiting overloaded defenders.
notes.plans: Play Nfg5, threatening Nxf7 or Nxe6. If ...h6, Nxe6! deflects the f-pawn, and Qxg6+ leads to mate.

notes.explains: Black plays ...g6 to block the kingside. White considers two candidates: Qh3 (threatening ...h5, weakening Black) and Nf6+ (sacrificing the knight to open the f-file). Qh3 leaves the d4-pawn vulnerable; Nf6+ is safer and gives long-term attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between a risky attacking move and a solid one that maintains pressure, prefer the solid one if you don't see a forced win. Practical chess is about managing risk.
notes.plans: Play Nf6+! Bxf6 exf6, opening the f-file and creating a monster pawn on f6. Then bring the rook to f1 and queen to h3/h6, aiming for the 'lobster pincer' mate (pawn on f6, queen on h6, mate on g7).

notes.explains: After Nxe6 and Qxg6+, Black's king is exposed. White wins the exchange and keeps attacking. The key is not to rest after winning material; continue pressing for mate.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, don't simplify automatically. Keep attacking if the opponent's king is still vulnerable.
notes.plans: Bring the rook to f1, develop the queenside (e.g., Bf4, Rae1), and look for ways to infiltrate with the queen or rook.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd6, defending f8 and threatening ...Qxd4+. White cannot play c5 immediately because of ...Nxc5, attacking the queen. Instead, White should develop with Bf4!, winning the exchange on f8 and maintaining the attack.
notes.teaches: When your attack stalls, bring in more pieces. A quiet developing move with tempo (like Bf4) can be more effective than forcing moves.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, threatening Bxd6 or Bxc7. After ...Rxf6, recapture with the bishop, then bring the rook to e1 and continue the attack.

notes.explains: White wins the queen for a rook and bishop, but Black has some counterplay. White now brings the rook to e1, threatening infiltration. The key is to avoid trades and keep attacking.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, avoid unnecessary complications. Use your extra material to simplify only when it leads to a clear win.
notes.plans: Play Qe3, threatening Qxe6+ or c5. If ...Nxc5, Qxc5 wins. Alternatively, Qxc6 is strong because the f7-pawn is pinned.

notes.explains: White plays Qxc4, winning a pawn and keeping the attack. The f7-pawn is pinned, so Black cannot recapture. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a piece is pinned and exploit it. Here, the f7-pawn is pinned by the rook on e1, so Qxc6 is safe.
notes.plans: Continue attacking with the queen and rook, aiming for mate or further material gain.

notes.explains: Black commits to the King's Indian by playing d6, choosing a traditional setup against White's fianchetto variation.
notes.teaches: The King's Indian Defense is a hypermodern opening where Black allows White to build a broad center, then counterattacks.
notes.plans: Black will aim for e5 to challenge White's center, typical of King's Indian setups.

notes.explains: Black chooses the setup with Nbd7 and e5, a traditional King's Indian approach against the fianchetto.
notes.teaches: Against the fianchetto, Black has several setups: preparing e5, playing c5 (Bologan-style), or flexible systems like c6, Bf5, or Nc6 with a6 (Panno).
notes.plans: Black will push e5 and later consider c6 and Qa5 to create tactical threats.

notes.explains: Black plays c6 and Qa5, an older but tricky line. The queen on a5 attacks c3, preventing b3 and threatening to swing to h5.
notes.teaches: The queen on a5 serves multiple purposes: it prevents b3 (defending c4), can later go to h5 or b4, and creates tactical ideas like Nxe4 or Qc5 forking pieces.
notes.plans: Black will follow with e5, then recapture on d4 with the knight, aiming for a Maroczy-like structure with pressure on White's center.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, a modern recommendation. Black releases the tension with exd4, as delaying allows White to close the center with d5.
notes.teaches: When White has Be3, Black should exchange on d4 before White can push d5, which would cramp Black. The timing of pawn exchanges is critical.
notes.plans: After exd4, White can recapture with Bxd4 or Nxd4. Black will then aim to activate the knight via e5 or c5.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne5, establishing a strong outpost. White responds with Nd2, protecting c4 and preparing f4.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, a knight on e5 is a powerful asset. White often tries to dislodge it with f4, but Black can discourage this with g5, a risky but principled move.
notes.plans: Black plays g5 to prevent f4. If White plays f4 anyway, Black trades on f4 and retreats the knight to g6, pressuring f4 and creating tactical complications.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, a risky but principled move to prevent f4. White cannot easily play f4 now due to Black's counterplay.
notes.teaches: g5 weakens f5 and the kingside, but it also opens the g6 square for the knight and creates a bind. In the King's Indian, such pawn pushes are often necessary to maintain piece activity.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with h5 and g4 to cement the kingside bind, then target White's king with rook lifts and bishop maneuvers.

notes.explains: White plays hxg4, a mistake. Black now has the h-file open and can aim for Nh7-g5, targeting f3.
notes.teaches: When White captures on g4, it opens the h-file for Black and allows the knight to reroute to g5 via h7. White should have played h4 to freeze the h-file and restrict the knight.
notes.plans: Black plays Nh7, preparing Ng5. White tries to prevent it with Be3, but Black reinforces with Qe7, and eventually plays Ng5, creating threats on f3 and h3.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh7, aiming for Ng5. White plays Be3 to prevent it, but Black reinforces with Qe7.
notes.teaches: When a knight maneuver is threatened, White may try to block it. Black can reinforce the idea by defending the knight or creating additional threats.
notes.plans: Black eventually plays Ng5, and after White's defensive moves, Black trades dark-squared bishops to weaken White's kingside and then delivers a decisive attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxh6, trading dark-squared bishops. This weakens White's kingside and allows Black's knight to dominate.
notes.teaches: Trading the opponent's good bishop (the fianchettoed bishop) can leave the king vulnerable. In the King's Indian, the dark-squared bishop is often a key defender.
notes.plans: After the trade, Black's knight on g5 is very strong. Black will follow with Qh6, then Nh3+ forcing the exchange, and finally a queen checkmating attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh3+, forcing White to capture. After gxh3, Black recaptures with the queen, threatening Qh2#.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, knight checks can force the exchange of a defender, opening the door for a queen attack.
notes.plans: Black will deliver a staircase checkmate: Qh2+, Qg1+, Qg2+, driving the king to e1, then Rd8+ picks off the king.

notes.explains: The game was decided by subtle positional nuances. White's mistake was playing hxg4 instead of h4, which allowed Black's knight to reach g5.
notes.teaches: At high levels, games are decided by small margins. Prophylactic moves like h4, which restrict the opponent's pieces, can be decisive.

notes.explains: Against c4, the most principled response is …e5, treating the position as a reversed Sicilian. This avoids transpositions into other openings and leads to rich, strategic play.
notes.teaches: When facing the English, committing to e5 is the most ambitious and principled approach, forcing White to prove their understanding of reversed Sicilian structures.
notes.plans: After c4 e5, Black should be ready to meet Nc3 with …Nf6, and then g3 d5, reaching a reversed Accelerated Dragon where Black is a tempo down but has clear plans.

notes.explains: After c4 e5 Nc3 Nf6 g3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2, Black should not play …Be6 because it allows d4, creating central tension Black is not ready for. Instead, …Nb6 is correct, preventing d4 and clamping down on that square.
notes.teaches: In reversed Sicilian positions, Black must prioritize preventing White's d2-d4 break. The knight retreat to b6 is a key prophylactic move.
notes.plans: After …Nb6, Black will play ...Nc6, ...Be7, ...0-0, and then develop the light-squared bishop to e6 or g4, depending on circumstances.

notes.explains: In the reversed Sicilian, Black's dark-squared bishop belongs on e7, not d6 or c5. On d6 it walks into d4; on c5 it is vulnerable to a3-b4, Ne4, or Qc2. The modest e7 is safe and solid.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a bishop, consider not only activity but also vulnerability to pawn advances and enemy piece attacks. Safety often trumps apparent activity.
notes.plans: After ...Be7, Black castles and then develops the other bishop, typically to e6.

notes.explains: When White plays e3, threatening d4, Black should not reflexively try to prevent it. After d4 exd4 exd4, the resulting IQP structure is favorable for Black because Black controls the d5 square and has easier development.
notes.teaches: Not all pawn breaks are equally dangerous; sometimes allowing an isolated queen pawn is fine if you can control the square in front of it and have active piece play.
notes.plans: After d4, Black will play ...Be6, ...Nc6, ...Qd7 or ...Bf6, piling up on d5 and preparing to blockade with a knight or bishop.

notes.explains: In the IQP position after d4, Black should not occupy d5 prematurely with a knight (e.g., ...Nd5) because that allows Nxd5 Qxd5 and then Ne5, harassing the queen. Instead, Black should control d5 with pieces like ...Be6 and ...Nb4, reserving the option to occupy later.
notes.teaches: Controlling a key square is often more important than occupying it. Occupying can allow the opponent to trade off the blockader and gain activity.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Nb4 to increase control over d5, then ...Bf6 or ...Qd7, and eventually ...Nd5 when the time is right.

notes.explains: When White plays Ng5, Black should not panic. The move looks threatening but is a 'paper tiger' because Black can simply play ...Bf5, keeping the pieces on and maintaining the pressure. The threat of ...Nxe3 is real, and White's knight on g5 becomes loose.
notes.teaches: Do not assume a piece is too valuable to trade; evaluate concrete tactics. A positional assumption (e.g., 'my knight on d5 is my best piece') can lead to blunders if the tactical justification for the trade exists.
notes.plans: After ...Bf5, Black threatens ...Nxe3, and White must retreat or lose material. Black then continues to press on the IQP.

notes.explains: After White blunders a piece with Ng5?, Black can win it by ...Nxe3, since the knight on g5 is hanging. Black gets the bishop pair and a pawn on e3 becomes a target. The IQP is gone, but Black's extra piece and active pieces decide.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplify by trading pieces and targeting weak pawns. The bishop pair is especially valuable in open positions.
notes.plans: Black will target the e3 pawn with ...Nc4, ...Re8, and if White pushes e4, the d4 pawn becomes weak. Black's extra piece dominates.

notes.explains: After White plays g2 (a passive move), Black can carve out a dark-square weakness with ...c5. If White takes on c5, Black recaptures with the bishop and gains an outpost on e5. If White pushes d5, the e5 square becomes a monster outpost for a knight or bishop.
notes.teaches: When you have a dark-squared bishop and the opponent has weakened dark squares, provoke a pawn move to create a permanent outpost. This is a universal idea seen in many openings, like the Caro-Kann.
notes.plans: Black plays ...c5, then ...Nc4-e5, occupying the e5 outpost. The knight on e5 dominates the board and neutralizes White's fianchetto bishop.

notes.explains: With a monster knight on e5 and an extra piece, Black's plan is simple: push the c-pawn to create a passed pawn. White's rook on b7 is not scary because Black can defend with ...Qc7 or ...Bd4, and eventually push ...c4-c3.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, focus on concrete plans like pawn promotion. Do not be distracted by opponent's threats that are not real; calculate and see if they can be ignored or parried simply.
notes.plans: Black pushes ...c4, ...c3, anchors the pawn with the bishop, then brings rooks to the c-file and forces White to give up material for the pawn.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black forces a queen trade with ...Qc8, then uses the rook to harass White's rook on b7. After ...Rf7, White's rook is forced away, and the c-pawn promotes.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, trade queens to reduce counterplay, then use your extra piece to support a passed pawn. Be precise: choose the right rook to avoid checks.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Rac8 (to avoid checks), then ...c3, ...Rfd8, ...c2, and if White's rook blocks, use the bishop to dislodge it.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6, white has many dangerous options including Bg5, Bc4, f3, Be3, a4, etc. The English Attack is defined by f3, preparing g4-g5 and a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: The English Attack aims to storm the kingside with g4-g5, while black typically attacks on the queenside. The move f3 secures e4 and prepares the pawn advance.
notes.plans: White will castle queenside and push g4, g5, h4. Black will counter on the queenside with b5, a5, and possibly d5.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 0-0 10.0-0-0, the main line is …Nbd7 followed by b5. An interesting sideline is …a5, aiming to push a4 and create queenside pressure.
notes.teaches: The sideline a5 avoids the heavily theoretical main lines. It aims to push a4, opening lines on the queenside and creating weaknesses in white's camp.
notes.plans: Black will play a4, then possibly Na6-c7 to challenge the bishop on b5, and later push d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: After …a5, white's best response is a4 to stop a4. Then black plays …Nc6 aiming for b4. White continues g4 Nb4 g5, and black's best is …Nh5 or the tricky …Ne8, preparing d5.
notes.teaches: The move a4 creates a hole on b4, which black can exploit with Nc6-b4. White's g4-g5 is standard, but black can respond with Ne8 to prepare d5 and counterattack.
notes.plans: Black will play d5 after appropriate preparation, opening lines against white's king. White should consider f4 instead of h4 to maintain control.

notes.explains: In the game, white played Bb5, the most popular human response to a5. Black replies …Na6, intending Nc7 to dislodge the bishop. After Kb1 Nc7 Bb6 Qb8 Ba4, black has two main options: …Ra6 or …d5.
notes.teaches: The knight maneuver Na6-c7 is thematic to challenge the bishop on b5. The queen move Qb8 unpins the knight and renews the threat of Nxb5. The pawn break d5 is a key idea to eradicate the weak d5 square and open lines.
notes.plans: Black should play d5, opening the center and activating the dark-squared bishop. If white captures on c7, black recaptures with the queen and continues with d5.

notes.explains: After …d5 exd5 Nfxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5, white's best is Bxc7 Qxc7 exd5. Black then plays …Rfd8, and if white plays dxe6, black has a queen sacrifice: …Rxd2 exf7+ Kxf7 Kxd2, leading to a complex but roughly equal position.
notes.teaches: The queen sacrifice on d2 is a recurring theme in the English Attack. It leads to an unbalanced position where black has activity for the queen. This line requires precise calculation.
notes.plans: After the queen sacrifice, black will have rook and bishop for the queen, with active play against white's king. White should aim to consolidate.

notes.explains: In the game, white played Nxd5? instead of Bxc7. This is a mistake. After …Nxd5 Qf2, black missed a winning continuation: …Bd8! (threatening Bb5) and if Bxd8, then …b5! winning a piece because both bishops are hanging.
notes.teaches: Avoid automatic recaptures. After Qf2, black should not automatically recapture on b6. Instead, Bd8 and b5 exploits the loose bishops and wins material.
notes.plans: Black should play Bd8, then b5, forcing white to lose a piece. If white tries desperado, black captures on b5 and maintains a winning attack.

notes.explains: Black played …Ra6 instead of Bd8, which was a mistake. After b5 Bxe7 bxa6, the position is roughly equal. Black missed a chance to play …bxa4, leading to a complex but promising attack.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a sacrifice, consider whether the opponent can consolidate. In the line with bxa4, black's attack is strong because white's king is exposed and black has piece activity.
notes.plans: After bxa4, black should play Nb4, threatening smothered mate, and then follow up with a3 and rook to the a-file. White's best defense is to counter-sacrifice the exchange.

notes.explains: After …Nxe7 Nc5 Rc6 Bb3 Bxb3 axb3 Rfc8, black has good play. White's best is Ne7! (not Nd3). After …Rxc2, black is winning because the king is weak and black has a4 and knight to f5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, even material down, the initiative can be decisive. Black's knight and pawns create lasting threats.
notes.plans: Black will play Nf5, then h5 to avoid back rank issues, then Nc4 and a4, opening lines against the king. White's rooks are passive.

notes.explains: Black played …h6, a good move to create luft. Then white played Rhd1, and black made a mistake with a4?, allowing …b4 and the knight to c5. Correct was Nf5, heading to d4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a potential outpost, prevent it. Here, a4 allowed b4, giving white the c5 square. Instead, Nf5 would have kept the knight active and avoided the outpost.
notes.plans: After Nf5, black can play g4 to challenge the knight, but white can reply with Nxe5, leading to liquidation and a draw. Black should avoid overzealous pawn pushes that create weaknesses.

notes.explains: After …b4 Nc5 Rd7 Nf5 c3 a3, black played …Rd6? Correct was …axb2, but black feared Rd7 trapping the queen. However, black has a defensive resource: …Rd8! (not Ra8) and if Rxd8+ Qxd8, white cannot take the queen due to back rank mate threats.
notes.teaches: In defensive positions, look for counterplay. Here, Rd8 allows the queen to escape and creates threats against white's king. Do not assume a trapped queen is lost without calculating.
notes.plans: After axb2, black should play Rd8, and if white plays Rg1 or Rf1, black's queen is trapped but can still fight with two rooks for the queen. The position is unclear.

notes.explains: Black played …Rd6, and white responded with g4, a mistake. White should have taken on a3 immediately. After …Rxd2 Rxd2, black's knight can go to h4, attacking f3, so white cannot take on a3. White then played …b3, and black got counterplay.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify if possible. White's g4 allowed the knight to become active. Taking on a3 would have kept the knight passive and maintained a winning position.
notes.plans: After b3, black's knight can go to c4, and the a3 pawn becomes a long-term weakness. Black should aim to activate the queen and create threats against white's king.

notes.explains: After …Qc6 Ka2 Nb7, white missed a winning move: Ne4! This move dominates the knight on b7, which is out of play. White then can slowly improve and win the b5 pawn.
notes.teaches: Play for domination. When an opponent's piece is badly placed, restrict it further. Ne4 prevents f5 and keeps the knight on b7 useless. This is a grandmaster-level concept.
notes.plans: White should play Ne4, then slowly improve with rook to d3, queen to d2, etc., eventually winning the b5 pawn. Black's knight is out of the game.

notes.explains: White traded knights with Nxb7 Kxb7, and the position became equal. Black then activated the queen with …Qf6, aiming for h4. White played Qe4 Qh4, and black's queen infiltrated.
notes.teaches: When material is equal, activity matters. Black's queen on h4 creates threats against white's king and ties down white's pieces. White's king on a3 is vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black will continue to harass the king with queen checks and threats, eventually forcing a win. White must defend carefully.

notes.explains: After …Qh4 Qb7 Qxh2+ Ka3 Rf8, white played Qe4? allowing …Qc2. White's last chance was c4, but even then black is slightly better. The game ended with …Qc2 Re3? Rd8! winning.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, look for the most active defense. c4 would have given white chances to hold. The final mistake Re3 allowed Rd8, threatening mate and winning.
notes.plans: Black should play Rd8, threatening mate on d2. White's only defense is to block with the rook, but then black checks and wins. The king is too exposed.

notes.explains: The immediate d4 is a mistake because Black plays Qh4+ and White cannot block with g3 due to the f-pawn. White must move the king to e2, which is dangerous.
notes.teaches: Never play d4 before Nf3 in the King's Gambit, as it allows a devastating queen check.
notes.plans: Black should play d5 after Qh4+, sacrificing a pawn to develop rapidly and attack the exposed white king.

notes.explains: Black plays d5 immediately, sacrificing a pawn to open lines and develop the bishop to g4 with check. White's king is stuck on e2.
notes.teaches: When the white king is exposed, sacrifice material to accelerate development and launch an attack.
notes.plans: Black aims to castle queenside and bring the knight to d7, targeting the white king. White's king will never be safe.

notes.explains: Nc3 is a Vienna-style move that allows Qh4+ and Ke2, then Nf3 chasing the queen. Black can play d5 anyway, sacrificing a pawn for rapid development.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, Black should still play d5, ignoring the threat to the e5 pawn. The exposed white king compensates for the material.
notes.plans: After d5, Black develops with Bg4, Bd6, and Nc6, threatening Nd4+ and targeting the white king.

notes.explains: Black ignores the threat to c7 and plays Nc6, threatening Nd4+. If White plays d4, Black castles and takes on f4, then Nf6 attacks the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When the white king is exposed, prioritize threats against the king over material. The knight on d5 is illusory because White's king is vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black will take on f4 and f3, winning the queen or delivering checkmate. White's position collapses despite the central pawns.

notes.explains: After Nxa8, Black plays Ne5, threatening to take on f3 and then Qh5+ winning the queen. White cannot stop this plan easily.
notes.teaches: Even when a piece is trapped, look for tactical threats that exploit the opponent's king safety. The knight on a8 is irrelevant if White's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Black will take on f3, then Qh5+ and capture the queen. The knight on a8 will be trapped, leaving Black with a winning position.

notes.explains: White plays d4, but Black executes the sacrifice on f3, then Qh5+ wins the queen. The king on a dark square prevents a discovered check from saving White.
notes.teaches: Always ensure the opponent's king cannot escape via discovered checks. Here, the dark-square king is crucial for the tactic to work.
notes.plans: Black wins the queen and remains with a material advantage and a weak white king.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black plays g5 to prevent the bishop on c1 from evacuating the knight on a8 via c7. This prophylactic move secures the trapped knight.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a trapped piece, use pawn moves to restrict the opponent's pieces and prevent rescue attempts.
notes.plans: Black will play Nf6, targeting e4, then Kc8 and Kb8 to free the knight. The knight on a8 is not going anywhere.

notes.explains: If White plays e5, Black meets with Nh6, then exf6 Bd6, aiming to develop kingside pieces quickly so that f7 does not trap the rook. The rook goes to c8, not f8, to avoid Bg7 fork.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to trap a rook, develop pieces to cover escape squares. Here, Bd6 prevents Bg7 and allows Rc8.
notes.plans: Black will pick up the pawn on f7 and the knight on a8, ending with two pieces for a rook and a dominant position.

notes.explains: Against Bc4, Black does not play Qh4+ because the king can go to f1, which is safer than e2. Instead, Black develops with Nc6.
notes.teaches: Do not automatically check if it helps the opponent improve their king. Here, Qh4+ would allow White to escape to f1 with a safer position.
notes.plans: Black will play Nc6, and if d4, then Qh4+ followed by d6, pinning the knight with Bg4 and forcing a queen trade.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black plays g5, supporting the pawn. The bishop on c4 is poorly placed, and Black will play h6 and Ne7, building a solid setup.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is on c4, the g5 push is safe because White cannot easily attack the pawn. Black's setup is solid and a pawn up.
notes.plans: Black will play Bg7, h6, Ne7, and castle, maintaining the extra pawn with no compensation for White.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd7, leaving e7 free for the knight and preparing Na5 to trade off the bishop on c4. This neutralizes White's compensation.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is a key attacking piece, aim to trade it off. Here, Na5 forces a favorable exchange.
notes.plans: After Na5, Black will trade bishops and castle, leaving White with no attack and a pawn deficit.

notes.explains: Bc4 blunders a pawn. Black can simply take on f4. If Qe2, Black plays Qe7 and White only wins back one pawn, leaving Black with a superior endgame.
notes.teaches: Always check if the opponent's move hangs a pawn. In the Schallopp, Bc4 is a common mistake that gives Black an easy advantage.
notes.plans: Black takes on f4, then plays d5 and c6, building a queenside pawn wedge. The bishop on c4 is out of play.

notes.explains: d3 is passive. Black plays d5, and if exd5, then Bxf4. The computer prefers Nc6 development, but d5 is fine.
notes.teaches: Against passive moves, strike in the center. d5 opens lines and challenges White's control.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nc6, Bb4 or Bg4, and maintain the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Nc3 is a main line. Black plays d5, striking the center. If exd5, then Nxd5 and Black can play Qe7+ or retreat the knight to b6.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, the central break d5 is key. It challenges White's pawn center and opens lines for Black's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nc6, Bg4, and consider queenside castling if White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: After the queen exchange, Black plays Be7, not Bd6. The point is that Bxf4 is a trap: if White takes, Black wins the bishop with ...g5.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, Be7 is a precise move that sets a trap. Always look for tactical opportunities when recapturing pawns.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nc6, and if White plays c4, the queen drops back to d6 or f6. Black aims to castle and use the d5 outpost.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the f4 pawn to get quick development. The bishop on e6 will go to d5, a fantastic outpost, and White's center is weak.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is worth giving back the pawn to activate your pieces and create long-term positional trumps like an outpost.
notes.plans: Black will castle queenside and target White's weak pawns. The knight on d5 is a monster.

notes.explains: If White plays Bd3, Black defends the f4 pawn with g5. White's bishop on d3 is passive, and Black maintains the extra pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is not threatening, simply hold the pawn and continue development.
notes.plans: Black will play Nc6, Qc7, and castle queenside, keeping the extra pawn.

notes.explains: After e5 Nh5 d4, Black plays d6, not d5. The reason is that d5 would allow c4, undermining Black's center. With d6, Black avoids that and prepares f6.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, the move d6 is more flexible than d5 because it prevents White from playing c4 and undermining the center.
notes.plans: Black will play g6 or g5, then Nc6, and eventually f6 to break White's center.

notes.explains: If White plays Bc4, Black takes on e5 and forces queen trade, then Bg4+ wins the pawn on f4. Black is a pawn up with a better endgame.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, trading queens often favors Black because White's king is exposed and Black has the extra pawn.
notes.plans: Black will develop and enjoy a pawn-up endgame with active pieces.

notes.explains: After Qe2, Black trades queens and then plays Nc6, threatening Nd4+ and targeting the f4 pawn. White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, centralize your pieces and create threats. The knight on c6 is well placed.
notes.plans: Black will take on f4 and maintain the extra pawn with active pieces.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the knight on d4 to win the f4 pawn and expose the white king. After Bxf4, Black has two pawns and a strong attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece sacrifice is justified to destroy the opponent's pawn structure and expose the king.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...O-O-O and ...Rd8, targeting the white king.

notes.explains: If White plays Be2 (a rare move by Shaw), Black plays Nc6 and then g6. The idea is to avoid g5 because of d5, which would be strong for White. g6 is safer.
notes.teaches: When the opponent targets the knight, use g6 to create a safe retreat and support the center. g5 can be met by d5, so g6 is more solid.
notes.plans: Black will play Bg7, O-O, and then f6 to break White's center.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to undermine White's center. The knight on h5 is safe via g7. Black's position is solid and active.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, the move f6 is a key break to challenge White's pawn center. The knight can retreat to g7 or f5.
notes.plans: Black will open the center and activate the bishops, targeting White's king.

notes.explains: After a forcing sequence, Black ends up with a monster pawn chain on the kingside and active bishops. The queen on e5 is well placed.
notes.teaches: In tactical melees, keep your pieces active and create pawn chains that restrict the opponent.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Qe7 and ...Bf5, with a dominant position. White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: After queen trade, Black has a knight vs bishop endgame with a pawn chain. Black's knight is active and White's pawns are weak.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, active pieces and pawn structure matter more than material. Black's knight on f5 is a monster.
notes.plans: Black will target White's weak pawns and use the knight to create threats.

notes.explains: Black's knight goes to d6, attacking the c4 pawn and eyeing e4. White's pawns are weak and Black has a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, centralize your knight and target weak pawns. The knight on d6 is perfectly placed.
notes.plans: Black will win the c4 pawn and then advance the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: If White plays Bc4, Black trades queens and then plays Bg4+ and Nc6, threatening Nd4. White's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use checks and threats to prevent them from castling.
notes.plans: Black will take on f4 and develop with ...O-O-O, attacking the white king.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the knight on d4 to expose the king and deliver a check with ...O-O-O+. White's king is under attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is in the center, use sacrifices to open lines and bring your rook into the attack.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Rd8 and ...Bxf4, with a winning attack.

notes.explains: After a complex sequence, Black ends up with a rook and two pawns for two pieces, but the white king is exposed and Black has a strong attack.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, material is not the only factor. King safety and initiative matter more.
notes.plans: Black will continue the attack with ...Rd8 and ...Re8, targeting the white king.

notes.explains: Black's rooks double on the d-file, and the white king is chased to b6. Black has a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, double rooks on an open file to create mating threats.
notes.plans: Black will play ...R8d6 and ...Rb5+ to force checkmate or win material.

notes.explains: After a long forcing line, Black wins material and ends up with a rook and pawns against a knight. Black's pawns are strong.
notes.teaches: In complicated variations, stay calm and calculate accurately. The resulting endgame is winning for Black.
notes.plans: Black will advance the kingside pawns and use the rook to support them.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, challenging the center. White should not panic; the threat to c3 is not real because Qd2 pins the knight if it captures.
notes.teaches: When under pressure, look for tactical refutations before making defensive moves. Here, Qd2 wins the knight if it takes on c3.
notes.plans: Play Bd3, attacking the knight on f6 and preparing to castle. The open f-file will give attacking chances.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, preparing to fianchetto or play Ba6. White has a lead in development and an open f-file. The priority is to activate the dark-squared bishop with c4 and d5.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and an open file, you should open the center to increase the activity of your pieces, especially a bishop that is currently blocked.
notes.plans: Play c4, then d5, opening the diagonal for the bishop on b2. If Black does not develop, the attack will be overwhelming.

notes.explains: Black castles queenside, giving up the g7 pawn. White can take it, opening the g-file and starting a direct attack on the black king.
notes.teaches: When attacking, do not be afraid to take material if it is safe. Capturing a pawn can open lines and increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Take on g7 with Qxg7, then calculate the consequences: after ...Rg8, the queen escapes via f7, taking another pawn. Be ready to defend g2 if needed.

notes.explains: Black plays the quiet Rd8, a high-level move that does not threaten anything directly but prepares to trap the queen if she takes on f6. The queen is safe on f7 for now.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best defensive moves are quiet and prophylactic, not immediately threatening. They restrict the opponent's options and set subtle traps.
notes.plans: White should consolidate, defend g2, and look for ways to improve the position. Options include c5 to block the bishop, Nf4 to defend g2, or Rf2.

notes.explains: White takes another pawn with Bxh7, but this is a panicky move. The bishop was a key defender; better was Rf2 or c5 to consolidate.
notes.teaches: When under attack, do not grab material at the cost of your position's integrity. Sometimes consolidating moves (like Rf2) are more important than winning a pawn.
notes.plans: After Bxh7, Black can play c5, opening the diagonal and threatening the queen. White must defend g2 carefully.

notes.explains: White retreats the queen to d3, a safe square that defends the king and keeps the queen active. The rook on f2 defends g2.
notes.teaches: When defending, place your queen on a safe square where it can both defend and potentially counterattack. Avoid putting the queen on the edge where it can be trapped.
notes.plans: Consolidate with Rf2, keep the bishop on b2 for potential activity, and wait for Black to overextend.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, attacking the bishop. White retreats to b2, and Black plays Rd8, putting pressure on the queen. White's knight on d2 is passive.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates threats, do not panic. Find a safe square for your pieces and try to maintain tension. Here, the bishop on b2 is safe and the queen can go to e3.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like Qe3, which is safe and prevents Qc5. The position is complex but defensible.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a knight on e4, creating a powerful attack. White cannot take the queen due to Nf3+ and loss of the queen. This is a brilliant tactical idea.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece sacrifice can completely disrupt the opponent's coordination. Always consider such sacrifices when your pieces are well-placed and the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: White must find a defense. Options include Kh1, Qb3, or Bc3, but all are met with strong counterplay. The position is very difficult for White.

notes.explains: White plays Kh1, a desperate defensive move that prepares Rg1 to defend g2. It is a 'curl up into a ball' strategy, making it hard for Black to break through.
notes.teaches: When under a fierce attack, sometimes you must make ugly defensive moves to survive. Creating a fortress-like structure can frustrate the opponent and lead to mistakes.
notes.plans: After Kh1, White hopes to play Rg1 and defend g2. Black should continue the attack with moves like Qd5 or Rg8, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd5, threatening Rxg2. White's Rg1 is met by Rxg2+ and then Rg8, winning the rook. This is a crushing sequence.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for sequences that force the opponent's pieces to defend each other, then exploit the overload. Here, the rook on g1 is overloaded.
notes.plans: Black should continue the attack, eventually winning material. White can only delay the loss.

notes.explains: White tries Ng5 to block the g-file, but Black simply takes it. The attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a strong attack, desperate measures often fail. It is better to find the most resilient defense early on.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press, eventually converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black avoids taking the bishop, instead playing Rg8, maintaining pressure. This is a high-level decision to keep the attack going rather than win material.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, sometimes it is better to keep the attack than to cash in material immediately. This prevents counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should continue to threaten mate or win more material. White is in zugzwang.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne2, winning the queen. The endgame is technically winning for Black, but requires precise technique.
notes.teaches: Even in a winning endgame, you must be careful not to allow stalemate or a fortress. Here, Black must avoid pushing the pawn to a2 prematurely, as that could lead to a draw.
notes.plans: Black should advance the pawns carefully, using the knight to control key squares, and avoid stalemate traps.

notes.explains: White's Qh5 attacks e5 but does not defend e4, and the queen becomes a target. Black should develop naturally rather than panic-defend the c5-pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes an early queen sortie, the best response is often to continue developing with tempo, trusting that the queen will become vulnerable.
notes.plans: Develop Nf6, attacking the queen and preparing to occupy the center with d5 or e6.

notes.explains: Bc4 threatens checkmate on f7. The best defense is e6, which blocks the bishop but prepares a solid pawn center with d5. The light-squared bishop may be passive on d7, but that is acceptable.
notes.teaches: Not every piece needs to be active immediately. A temporarily passive bishop is a small price to pay for a safe king and a strong center.
notes.plans: Play e6, then d5, followed by Bc5 (attacking f2) and castling kingside.

notes.explains: White's d3 is a mistake because it allows Nd4, forking the queen and bishop. The queen on f3 is vulnerable, and Nd4 creates multiple threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is exposed, look for forks and double attacks that exploit its vulnerability.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, threatening Nxc2+ and the bishop on b5. After Qd1, capture the bishop with Nxb5, winning a pawn and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Nc3 develops with tempo, attacking the queen. This highlights the fundamental weakness of the Scandinavian: Black moves the queen multiple times, falling behind in development.
notes.teaches: Develop with tempo whenever possible. Punish early queen moves by gaining time and central control.
notes.plans: After Qe6+, block with Be2, then play Nf3, d4, and castle kingside, building a massive lead in development.

notes.explains: Black's Bd7 is a serious mistake because it does nothing to address the development deficit. White can now play Nf3, d4, and castle, while Black's queen remains a target.
notes.teaches: In the opening, every move should either develop a piece, control the center, or improve king safety. Wasting time with passive moves like Bd7 is fatal.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then d4 (threatening d5 forking queen and knight), castle, and exploit Black's undeveloped kingside.

notes.explains: d4 threatens d5, forking the queen on e6 and the knight on c6. Black's queen has no good square: Qd6 loses to Nb5, and Qg6 allows d5 with a strong attack.
notes.teaches: A pawn fork in the center can be devastating when the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated. Always look for such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Push d5, winning material or forcing a decisive positional concession. If Black plays Qd6, Nb5 wins the queen. If Qg6, continue with d5 and develop with tempo.

notes.explains: After e4 d5 exd5 Nf6, White cannot keep the extra pawn with c4 because Black replies …c6, leading to either a Panov–Botvinnik Attack or dxc6 Nxc6 with a strong center and a bad light-squared bishop for White.
notes.teaches: In the Scandinavian, White should not cling to the pawn; instead, seek active development with tempo.
notes.plans: Play Bb5+ to provoke a weakening move, then retreat to e2 to prevent ...Bg4.

notes.explains: Bb5+ is a developing move with tempo. Black's best reply is …Bd7, which blocks the b8-knight and cuts communication between queen and center, making the bishop poorly placed.
notes.teaches: Provoke the opponent into making a move that impairs their own development.
notes.plans: After …Bd7, retreat the bishop to e2 to prevent ...Bg4, then build the center with d4.

notes.explains: Be2 is necessary to stop ...Bg4, which would attack the queen and improve Black's bishop. Moving the bishop also prevents Black from trading it off later with ...a6 and ...Bxb5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must retreat a piece to a less active square to neutralize a threat and maintain your structural advantage.
notes.plans: Follow with d4, then Nf3, O-O, and c4 to challenge the knight on d5.

notes.explains: After Nf3 Nf6 d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Bg2 O-O O-O d5 c4 dxc4 Na3 c3 bxc3 c5, we reach a tabia. Black has sacrificed the c-pawn to damage White's queenside structure, leaving a backward pawn on c3 and an isolated a-pawn.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is doomed, give it up on your own terms to force structural weaknesses in the opponent's camp.
notes.plans: Black must immediately counter in the center with ...c5 to prevent White from consolidating with e4. The position is dynamically balanced, with Black aiming to pressure d4 and White trying to solidify the center.

notes.explains: White plays Rb1, preparing e4. Black should not fear White's central expansion; instead, Black should encourage it to create targets.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld, allowing White to advance in the center can be beneficial because it makes the d4 pawn more vulnerable and opens lines for Black's pieces.
notes.plans: Black develops naturally with ...Nc6, pressuring d4. If White plays e4, Black can develop the light-squared bishop to g4, pinning the knight and increasing pressure on d4.

notes.explains: After …Nc6, White played h3 to prevent ...Bg4. Black should not play ...Bf5 immediately because it leaves b7 undefended and allows White annoying replies like Qb3 or Ne5.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, avoid premature bishop sorties that weaken your pawn structure. Develop solidly first.
notes.plans: Black can consider ...Qa5, pressuring c3 and vacating d8 for the rook, or ...Bf5 if the tactics work out. The key is to maintain pressure on the center while ensuring piece safety.

notes.explains: Black plays …Qa5, attacking c3 and preparing ...Rd8. The queen also x-rays the rook on e1, which can become important if White's rooks become disconnected.
notes.teaches: Always look for x-rays and deflection tactics. If the opponent's rooks are unconnected, a queen on the a5-e1 diagonal can create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Black continues with ...Rd8 to increase pressure on d4. White must defend c3, and Black will look for ways to undermine the center.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3 instead of c3, allowing Black to capture on d4. White then develops Bd3, ignoring the pawn deficit, to maintain the clamp on e5 and prepare kingside play.
notes.teaches: In closed structures, rapid development and piece activity can outweigh material concerns. The e5 pawn acts as a clamp, restricting Black's development.
notes.plans: White aims to complete kingside development quickly, then win back the d4 pawn with Nb1-d2-b3, while keeping the e5 pawn intact.

notes.explains: White castles and develops the knight to b3, pressuring d4 and preparing to recapture the pawn. Black's bishop on c5 retreats to b6 to avoid exchanges.
notes.teaches: The knight on b3 is ideally placed: it attacks d4, does not block the bishops, and supports a future Greek Gift sacrifice on h7.
notes.plans: White will eventually win back the d4 pawn, often after Black castles into a Greek Gift attack. If Black delays castling, White can still regain the pawn with Nb3xd4.

notes.explains: Black avoids the Greek Gift by delaying castling and playing Bd7. White can still win back the pawn with Nb3xd4, and after Nxd4 Bxd4, White has a slight edge due to Black's bad bishop on c8.
notes.teaches: When the Greek Gift is not available, White can still regain the pawn and maintain pressure. The bishop on d3 remains active, and Black's French bishop is a long-term weakness.
notes.plans: Play h3 to prevent ...Qg5, then recapture on d4, followed by c3 to support the knight and leave Black with a passive bishop.

notes.explains: After d4 g6 e4 Bg7 Nc3 c6, Black has entered the Gurgenidze System, a hybrid of the Caro-Kann and Modern. White's main move is f4, but a practical alternative is Be3, reserving f3 for later.
notes.teaches: Delaying f4 in favor of Be3 is flexible: it develops a piece and keeps options open, while f3 can be played later to support the center and restrict Black's knight.
notes.plans: Play f3 next to build a strong pawn center, then develop queenside and prepare to castle long.

notes.explains: After …d5, the position resembles the Fantasy Variation of the Caro-Kann, but with White's knight on c3 and bishop on e3 already developed—both are ideal squares for that structure.
notes.teaches: When Black plays d5 in this system, White's setup (Nc3, Be3) fits naturally with the Fantasy plan: the bishop belongs on e3 and the knight on c3 in that variation.
notes.plans: Play f3 to support e4 and prepare to develop the kingside, then consider e5 or other central breaks.

notes.explains: With f3 played, White solidifies the center. Black's knight on g8 often struggles: Nh6 is met by Qd2 (protecting f5), and Nf6 runs into e5, forcing the knight to an awkward square like d7.
notes.teaches: In this structure, Black's knight development is problematic because natural squares (h6, f6) are easily punished. Delaying e5 keeps the knight out of play.
notes.plans: Continue developing, aiming for Qd2 and long castling, while keeping the option of e5 to harass Black's knight.

notes.explains: Black's …e5 opens the center prematurely. White is ahead in development, so blasting open lines favors the better-developed side. After dxe5, Black cannot play d4 because White has two defenders (Nc3, Be3) against one attacker.
notes.teaches: When your opponent opens the center while behind in development, you should welcome it. Always check if a central pawn push like d4 is possible—here it's impossible due to superior control.
notes.plans: Capture on e5, then consider capturing on d5 or developing with Qd2 and long castling.

notes.explains: After Qd2, Black cannot play d4 because the queen hangs with checkmate. If Black plays Nc6, White has Bb5, pinning the knight and indirectly defending d4. This tactical nuance makes Qd2 safe and effective.
notes.teaches: When calculating, always check if your opponent's pawn push is possible. Here, d4 is impossible due to the queen's alignment with the king. Also, pins can be used to indirectly defend key squares.
notes.plans: Continue with O-O-O, then bring the knight to d4 to blockade the IQP, and prepare kingside attack with h4 or g4.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd7, preparing queenside castling. White can continue improving with Kb1 (king safety) or Bb5 (pinning the knight). Both are good; the choice is a matter of taste and time management.
notes.teaches: When two moves are similarly good, don't spend excessive time deciding. Use intuition and time management; the decision is unlikely to decide the game.
notes.plans: Play Kb1 to secure the king, then continue with Rde1 or h4. Alternatively, Bb5 to pin the knight and prevent Nxd4.

notes.explains: White's Qxd4 is a poor move in the Sicilian because it loses tempi, essentially playing a Scandinavian Defense with colors reversed but with a pawn already on e4, which is worse for White.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, White should avoid early queen sorties that waste time; development and central control are paramount.
notes.plans: Black should attack the queen with Nc6, forcing it to move again, gaining time.

notes.explains: After …a5, Black prevents b4 but weakens b5. White's king is on d1, and the c5 pawn is hanging. The position is sharp; White must decide how to handle the extra pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn but your king is exposed, prioritize development and piece activity over clinging to the pawn at all costs. Look for flexible moves that create threats and improve your pieces.
notes.plans: Play Na3, aiming for Nb5, threatening Nc7+ and forcing concessions. If Black plays e6/e5, jump to b5 and then possibly d6, securing the bishop pair and dark-square control.

notes.explains: Na3 is a flexible developing move that prepares Nb5. It avoids immediate pawn defense and instead creates a threat (Nc7+) that forces Black to react. This is more effective than passive defense like Be3 or a3.
notes.teaches: When defending a weak pawn, indirect methods (creating threats) are often superior to direct defense. A knight on b5 can be a powerful outpost, especially when the black queen is gone.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nb5, then either Nc7+ or Nd6, depending on Black's response. If Black plays Nd5, consider Bc4 or c4 to challenge the knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd5, covering c7 but the knight is unstable. White has two good options: Bc4 (simple development, threatening to trade and secure the c5 pawn) or Nb5 (more aggressive, threatening c4 and Bc4). Nb5 is particularly strong because it forces Black to make concessions to defend c7.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on d5, it can be a target. Use pawn breaks (c4) or piece pressure (Bc4, Nb5) to challenge it. A knight on b5 creates a double threat (c4 and Nc7) that is hard to meet.
notes.plans: Play Nb5, threatening Nc7+. Black's best reply is Kd8, after which White can also consider Ng5, targeting f7. Alternatively, Bc4 is simpler and solid.

notes.explains: After Nb5 Kd8, Black has moved his king and cannot castle. White now has a strong initiative. Ng5 is a logical follow-up, hitting f7 and creating a double-knight attack on the kingside. Black must defend f7, often with g5, weakening further.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king has moved, double-knight attacks (Nb5 and Ng5) can be devastating. Don't be afraid to play aggressively; knights can retreat if needed.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, threatening Nxf7. If Black plays g5, then f4 can open lines. Alternatively, Bc4 is simpler and also strong.

notes.explains: Black plays Be6 to defend f7. White can immediately take on e6, ruining Black's pawn structure and creating doubled e-pawns. This is a permanent structural weakness for Black.
notes.teaches: When you have the chance to ruin the opponent's pawn structure with a capture, do it. Doubled pawns are a long-term liability, especially in the endgame.
notes.plans: Take on e6 with the knight (Nxe6), then develop the bishop to h3 or g4 to target the e6 pawn. The king can stay on d1 or move to e2.

notes.explains: After Nxe6 fxe6, Black has doubled e-pawns and a weak e6 pawn. White's king is safe on d1. The plan is to develop the bishop to h3 (via g3) to attack e6 and then bring the rook to d1, targeting the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: In positions with a structural advantage, focus on the weakest point. The e6 pawn is a target, but the immediate threat is the knight on d5, which can be attacked with Rd1.
notes.plans: Play g3, then Bh3, attacking e6. Then Rd1, threatening to win the knight on d5. If Black defends with Rd8, Nc7+ forks the rook.

notes.explains: g3 prepares Bh3, targeting e6. It also covers f4 and h4, restricting Black's knights. The move is more flexible than Be2-g4 because it also supports a future pawn push on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When choosing a development scheme, consider not only the immediate target but also the long-term control of squares. g3 and Bh3 is a prophylactic setup that also attacks.
notes.plans: Follow with Bh3, then Rd1. The threat of Rd1 is devastating because the knight on d5 has no good retreat and Black cannot castle.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, trying to free his position. White can simply take the pawn (Bxe5) because the bishop on h3 will prevent the black king from escaping to c8 after a check on d1.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create counterplay, be ready to capture material if it doesn't weaken your position. The bishop on h3 serves a dual purpose: attacking e6 and controlling the c8 square.
notes.plans: Take on e5 with the bishop, then play Rd1+. The king will be forced to e8, and then Nc7+ wins the rook.

notes.explains: After the main moves, Black has several options: Bg4, e6, Nc6, and others. The position is highly theoretical. White's plan is flexible, often involving Na3 and Nb5.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, White's setup is solid and flexible. The key is to develop quickly and target the c7 square with a knight on b5.
notes.plans: Against Bg4, consider h3 and then g4 to drive the bishop away. Against e6, play Na3 and Nb5. Against Nc6, dxc5 is strong.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3, we reach a key Alapin position. Black's queen on d5 is exposed, and White's c3 pawn supports d4 but blocks the knight's natural square. Black's best is Nf6, developing with a threat.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, White's c3 pawn prepares d4 to occupy the center, but it also restricts the b1 knight. Black's queen on d5 is vulnerable to harassment, so Black should develop quickly rather than capture on d4 prematurely.
notes.plans: White aims to develop naturally, waiting for Black to commit. If Black plays e6, White can consider unusual knight maneuvers like Na3 to target b5 and c7.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White can play h3, and if Bh5, then g4, forcing the bishop to retreat. This is a common idea to gain space and tempo.
notes.teaches: When your knight is pinned, don't be afraid to advance pawns to drive the bishop away. This can give you a space advantage and open lines.
notes.plans: Play h3, then g4, chasing the bishop to g6. Then develop with Nbd2 or Be2, and later target the f3 pawn if Black takes.

notes.explains: e6 is a solid move, preparing to develop the bishop. White's best is Na3, heading for b5. This is a standard plan in the Alapin.
notes.teaches: When Black plays e6, the knight on b5 becomes a powerful outpost. It threatens Nc7+ and forces Black to react.
notes.plans: Play Na3, then Nb5. If Black plays Qd8, then Qxd4 or Nxd4. If Black plays Na6, then White has a pleasant endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, a solid move that prepares kingside development (Be7, O-O) and leaves the c8 bishop for later. White now has a choice: standard development or the aggressive Na3.
notes.teaches: Against e6, White's most promising plan is Na3, with three ideas: (1) Nb5 threatening Nc7 fork, (2) preparing Bc4 with tempo, and (3) if Black plays a6, Nc4 targets the weak b6 square.
notes.plans: White plays Na3, intending Nb5 or Nc4 depending on Black's response. If Black allows Nb5, White follows with Bf4 to pressure c7.

notes.explains: After dxc5 Qxd1+ Kxd1, White has an extra pawn but the king is in the center. Black's best is e5 or Bg4. The endgame is tricky but favorable for White due to the c5 pawn and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to enter an endgame with the king exposed if you have a pawn advantage and active pieces. The king can often find safety later.
notes.plans: Develop quickly, aiming to secure the c5 pawn or trade it for positional gains. Na3 and Nb5 is a common plan.

notes.explains: e5 is a common move, trying to challenge White's center. White should play b4, gaining space and threatening to develop with tempo. If Black plays e4, the knight can go to d4.
notes.teaches: When Black pushes e5, respond with b4 to gain space on the queenside. This is a typical Alapin idea.
notes.plans: Play b4, then develop the bishop to e3 or b5. The king can go to c1 or b2 for safety.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White's best is Be3, developing and protecting the c5 pawn. If Black plays Nc5, then Bxc5 is possible, but the engine prefers Bc4.
notes.teaches: When Black pins the knight, develop the bishop to e3 to support the center and the c5 pawn. Be aware of tactical nuances like ...Nxe3 fxe3.
notes.plans: Play Be3, then consider h3 to drive the bishop away. If Black takes on f3, recapture with the pawn and use the open g-file.

notes.explains: Bd2 is a passive but recently popular move; White intends to recapture on c3 with the bishop to preserve queenside pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black often trades the bishop for the knight on c3 to weaken White's control over e4.
notes.plans: Black will develop with b6, Bb7, d6, and Nbd7, creating a solid, flexible setup.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, preparing Bb7 and a solid setup. This is a standard Nimzo-Indian plan, avoiding d5 which would be less thematic.
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian setup with b6, Bb7, d6, and Nbd7 is solid because it creates no weaknesses and gives Black easy development.
notes.plans: Continue with Bb7, d6, Nbd7, then consider either Qe7 followed by e5, or the more aggressive Ne4 and f5.

notes.explains: Black puts a knight on e4, a natural outpost. This is a typical idea in many openings, often followed by f5 to support the knight and start a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: A knight on e4 supported by f5 is a classic attacking structure; it pressures White and can lead to a kingside initiative.
notes.plans: After Ne4, play f5 to reinforce the knight and prepare further kingside expansion.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes the bishop to g7, but this is slow and the bishop will bite on White's pawn chain. White has several good moves, including Nc3 or Bc4. Bc4 forces Black to decide between retreating the knight or playing e6, which weakens dark squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is fianchettoed against a pawn chain, it often becomes a 'granite biter'—less effective. Exploit slow development with active piece play.
notes.plans: Play Bc4 to pressure f7 and force Black to weaken the dark squares. If Black plays e6, target the weakened d6 and f6 squares.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2 to avoid queen trades and support the center. This move also prepares to meet Bg4 with a tactical sequence: Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+ Kg8 Qxg4, winning a pawn and exposing Black's king.
notes.teaches: A queen move to e2 can simultaneously support the center, avoid trades, and set up tactical threats against a pin.
notes.plans: After Qe2, continue development with O-O and h3 to prevent Bg4. Then aim to build pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: After both sides castle, White plays h3 to prevent Bg4, which would pin the knight and threaten the center. The knight is an integral defender of the d4 and e5 pawns.
notes.teaches: Prevent pins that target key defenders of your pawn center. A pawn move like h3 can be more important than developing a queenside piece.
notes.plans: After h3, continue with Rook to d1 to support the d4 pawn and prepare to meet Qc7 with Bf4, developing and defending e5.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 attacking e5. White defends with Bf4, which develops the bishop, protects the pawn, and sets up an x-ray against Black's queen. The bishop can later retreat to h2 if needed.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for moves that accomplish multiple tasks: development, defense, and setting up future threats.
notes.plans: After Bf4, develop the queenside with Nc3, and consider Rd1 to pressure the queen. If Black plays Bf5, White can consider g4 to chase the bishop away, but a solid approach is Nc3.

notes.explains: Black plays Rfd8, a mistake. The rook on f8 was protecting f7, so White can now play Bxf7+ Kxf7, followed by e6+ discovering an attack on the queen. Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of which pieces are defending critical squares like f7. Moving a defender can create tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: After Bxf7+, if Kxf7, play e6+ forking king and queen. If Kh8, retreat the bishop to b3, sacrificing the exchange to keep the light-squared bishop active for the attack.

notes.explains: Black's Nc6 is a slight inaccuracy because after d4 cxd4 cxd4, White threatens d5, kicking the knight. Without pawn support, the knight lacks a foothold and can be driven back or trapped.
notes.teaches: In the opening, pawns should lead the way; bringing out knights before supporting pawns allows the opponent to chase them with tempo.
notes.plans: White will push d5 to gain space and displace the knight, then develop with Nf3 and Nc3.

notes.explains: Black's best response is d5, counterstriking in the center. After exd5 Qxd5, White must defend the d4 pawn with Nf3, not Nc3 (which hangs d4).
notes.teaches: When the queen appears early, prioritize protecting your central pawn over attacking the queen; Nf3 develops and defends d4 simultaneously.
notes.plans: After Nf3, White will develop Nc3, gaining a tempo on the queen, and then push d5 to create an isolated queen pawn (IQP) structure.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bg4, threatening to win the d4 pawn. The intuitive Be2 is too slow; White must play Nc3 immediately, forcing the queen to move.
notes.teaches: When the queen is on d5, Nc3 forces it away, and if it retreats, d5 becomes a devastating pawn push, kicking the knight and opening lines against the uncastled king.
notes.plans: Play Nc3, and if the queen moves, push d5 to gain space and create threats like Bb5+ or Qa4+.

notes.explains: Black's queen retreats to a5. White should immediately push d5, kicking the knight, because delaying allows black to play e6, blunting the pawn push.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the pawn push d5 is a critical lever; play it before black can solidify with e6.
notes.plans: Push d5, forcing the knight to move, then exploit the open lines with Bb5+ or Qa4+ to harass the black king.

notes.explains: Black's knight goes to e5. White can play Bb5+ to force the king to move or block, exploiting black's lack of development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, checks and tempo-gaining moves can create a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Play Bb5+, forcing either Kd8 (disastrous) or a block that weakens black's position further.

notes.explains: Black's king is forced to d8, a terrible square. White has a massive lead in development and can continue with Qe2 or Nxe5, opening lines.
notes.teaches: When the king is forced to the center, every tempo counts; bring out pieces quickly and avoid trading queens unless it wins material.
notes.plans: Develop with Qe2 or Nxe5, then castle and bring rooks to open files to attack the exposed king.

notes.explains: Black castles queenside, but the king on c8 is vulnerable due to the open c-file. White can play Bd2 to unpin the pawn and set up an x-ray against the queen.
notes.teaches: Queenside castling in an open c-file is risky; use the open file to attack the king with rook to c1.
notes.plans: Play Bd2, threatening to win the queen or force a favorable trade, then bring the rook to c1.

notes.explains: Bd2 unpins the d5 pawn and threatens Nxb5, attacking the queen. Black must deal with this threat, often by moving the queen or playing e6.
notes.teaches: Simple developing moves with a threat are often stronger than flashy tactics; they maintain pressure without risk.
notes.plans: After black responds, continue developing with Bc4 or O-O, preparing to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: Black exchanges bishop for knight. White can recapture with the queen (Qxf3) or the g-pawn (gxf3). Qxf3 is positionally sound, keeping pawn structure intact, while gxf3 opens lines for attack.
notes.teaches: When deciding between recaptures, consider pawn structure and king safety; gxf3 can be aggressive but weakens the kingside.
notes.plans: If Qxf3, centralize the queen to e4 or f5, pressuring the knight and preventing counterplay. If gxf3, use the open g-file for attack.

notes.explains: Black's knight jumps to e5, attacking the queen. White can play Qe4 or Qf5, both centralizing the queen and threatening the knight.
notes.teaches: Centralize the queen to active squares where it cannot be easily attacked; avoid giving the opponent tempo with pointless queen moves.
notes.plans: Play Qe4, covering c2 and attacking the knight; if the knight retreats, continue developing with Bd3 or O-O.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to d7. White should avoid automatic moves like Bb5, which allows black to trade queens and ease the defense. Instead, play Bd3, developing and preparing Nxb5.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, prefer simple, solid moves that maintain pressure; avoid trades that relieve the opponent's congestion.
notes.plans: Play Bd3, reinforcing the threat of Nxb5, then castle kingside and bring the rook to e1 to attack the black king.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop and castle. White should continue developing with O-O, then bring the rook to e1, targeting the e7 pawn and the king.
notes.teaches: Patience is key; keep building pressure with simple moves like castling and rook activation. The opponent will eventually crack under the strain.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then play Re1, threatening to open the e-file. If black castles, the e-file attack remains strong.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes and is close to castling. White must prevent this. A good move is Be3, forcing the queen to a worse square, or Re1, doubling on the e-file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is about to complete development, use prophylactic moves to disrupt their plans. Blocking the e-file with Be3 can be counterintuitive but effective if it forces the queen to a bad square.
notes.plans: Play Be3, attacking the queen. If the queen moves to b6 or d8, follow with Bd4, dominating the long diagonal and pressuring the knight.

notes.explains: Black's queen goes to b6. White can play Bd4, attacking the queen and threatening to win the knight on d7. The bishop on d4 is powerful on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on long diagonals where they pressure the opponent's pieces and restrict the king's escape.
notes.plans: Play Bd4, forcing the queen to move. If the queen takes on b2, White has tactical resources like Qc7 or Rc1 to win material.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne4, the principled response, challenging the bishop immediately. White often replies h4 (Hodgson variation), intending to recapture with the h-pawn if Black takes on g5, opening the h-file and freezing Black's kingside pawns.
